title: A test that passes once proves less than it used to
description: Why exact-match assertions against a generative call are testing the wrong thing, and why weakening them into vacuous checks is worse than deleting the test.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why exact-string assertions against generative output are unreliable
Distinguish a weakened assertion from a genuinely fixed one

contentSections.title: A green suite, a broken tool

contentSections.body:
A support-ticket summarizer's CI pipeline goes green — every unit test passes — and the team deploys. Two days later a customer forwards a summary claiming "as agreed, we'll refund the full amount within 24 hours." Nobody agreed to that. The refund policy the model described doesn't exist anywhere in the codebase, the prompt, or the ticket it summarized.

The test suite genuinely covered the code. Nothing in it ran the actual model on a real ticket.

contentSections.scenario:
The summarizer's one existing test calls the tool with a fixed sample ticket and asserts the output string equals exactly:

`"Customer reports login failure on mobile app, requests password reset."`

A teammate reruns the exact same test the next morning against the exact same ticket. The assertion fails — the output this time is `"Customer is unable to log in via the mobile app and has requested a password reset."` Same meaning, different wording.
contentSections.question: Is the failing test catching a real bug?

options.label: Yes — the output changed, so something is broken
No — the test is asserting something the tool was never designed to guarantee
Can't tell without seeing the model's system prompt

feedback.bug: Nothing about the tool's behavior changed — it still correctly identified a login failure and a reset request, which is the actual job. What changed is the exact string, and the test conflated "the same string" with "correct." That's the test's assumption, not the tool's defect.
feedback.test: Right. A generation call at any temperature above zero (and often even at zero — more on that next lesson) can phrase the same correct answer two different ways. An assertion of exact string equality is really asserting "the model must phrase this identically every time," which was never a real requirement of the tool. The test is measuring the wrong thing.
feedback.unclear: The system prompt doesn't change the underlying fact: exact-string equality is the wrong assertion for a generative call regardless of how it's prompted. You don't need to see it to know the test is fragile.

contentSections.concept: **Traditional testing assumes: same input in, same output out, always.** A generative model call breaks the second half of that for anything beyond a trivial, tightly-constrained prompt. The fix isn't to give up on assertions — it's to assert the thing that's actually supposed to stay stable (did it identify the failure type, the requested action, the customer's account) instead of the thing that isn't (the exact sentence).

contentSections.body: This is the core shift the rest of the phase works from: a test against an AI-dependent function can't ask *"is this the output"* anymore. It has to ask *"is this a valid output"* — which means deciding, before you write the assertion, what actually has to be true of a correct response and what's just one of many acceptable phrasings of it. That decision is real design work, not a formality, and skipping it is how a team ends up with a test suite that's either too brittle to survive a Tuesday or too loose to catch the ticket that invents a refund policy.
A test that asserts exact output text isn't testing the tool's correctness — it's testing whether the model phrased things identically to last time, which was never a real requirement.

contentSections.title: The fix that isn't a fix

contentSections.body: Faced with the failing exact-match test, an engineer under deadline pressure changes the assertion from `output === expected` to `output.length > 0`. The suite goes green again. It now passes for literally any non-empty response — including the one that promised a refund that doesn't exist.

contentSections.question: What's wrong with weakening the assertion this way?

options.label: length > 0 is too strict — it should check for a minimum word count instead
It no longer asserts anything the tool actually needs to get right
Nothing — a loose assertion is the correct response to non-determinism

feedback.strict: A minimum word count has the same underlying problem — it's still not checking anything about whether the summary is *correct*, just that it's long enough to look plausible.
feedback.vacuous: Right. The test now passes for a summary that hallucinates a refund policy, one that summarizes the wrong ticket entirely, or one that's just the word "error" repeated forty times — anything non-empty. It went from asserting the wrong thing to asserting almost nothing. The green checkmark is now actively misleading: it tells the team the suite caught a real problem when it structurally cannot.
feedback.correct: Non-determinism is a real reason to change *what* you assert, not a reason to stop asserting anything meaningful. There's a large space between "exact string match" and "non-empty string" — this lesson and the next two are about finding it.

contentSections.flawExplanation:
This is the failure mode to watch for across the whole phase: weakening an assertion until it stops failing is not the same as fixing it, and a suite that's all green because nothing in it can fail anymore is worse than no suite — it's a false signal that someone will trust.

The honest fix here isn't a looser string check. It's asserting the things that actually have to be true: does the output mention the customer's real issue (login failure), does it mention the actual requested action (password reset), and — critically — does it *avoid* introducing any commitment (refund, timeline, promise) that wasn't in the source ticket. That last one is checkable even against a model that phrases things differently every run.

contentSections.body: A rewritten assertion for the same test might check three separable things instead of one exact string: that the output contains no dollar amounts or promises not present in the input ticket, that it references the actual reported issue category (a login problem, extracted from the ticket's own tags), and that it's under some reasonable length so it's actually a summary and not a restatement. None of those require the wording to match anything — each one would have caught the invented refund policy on day one.
Loosening an assertion until the test stops failing isn't a fix — it's deleting the test while keeping the green checkmark.

title: What stays deterministic even when the model isn't
description: Separating a tool's ordinary, testable-the-normal-way code from the one genuinely non-deterministic step — and why even temperature 0 doesn't make that step a pure function.

learningObjectives.text: Identify which parts of an AI-powered tool's pipeline are deterministic
Explain why temperature 0 reduces but doesn't eliminate output variation

contentSections.title: Most of the tool isn't the model

contentSections.body: The same summarizer tool: a ticket comes in, gets validated and parsed, a prompt gets assembled from a template, the API call goes out, the JSON response gets parsed into a typed object, that object gets written to the database, and a Slack notification fires. Six steps. Exactly one of them involves the model deciding anything.

contentSections.scenario: Here are the six steps in the summarizer's pipeline.
contentSections.question: Select every step whose correctness you can test the ordinary way — fixed input, exact expected output, no model involved.

items.label: Validating that the incoming ticket has the required fields
Assembling the prompt string from the ticket data and a template
The API call itself deciding what the summary says
Parsing the model's JSON response into a typed Summary object
Writing the parsed Summary object to the database
Whether the summary is actually a good summary of the ticket

explanation.validate: Ordinary input validation — a fixed function of the ticket's shape. No model involved, fully deterministic.
explanation.template: String templating from known data is deterministic string manipulation. It's worth its own test precisely because a broken template (a missing field, a typo in a variable name) is a very common real bug that has nothing to do with the model and gets wrongly blamed on it.
explanation.call: This is the one genuinely non-deterministic step — what the model decides to say is not something a fixed-input, fixed-output test can pin down.
explanation.parse: Given a fixed, known JSON string (which you control in the test — you don't need a real API call to test this), parsing it into a typed object is ordinary code with a correct answer.
explanation.db: A database write given a fixed object is deterministic and testable the normal way — including testing what happens on a write failure.
explanation.quality: This is a judgment call about the model's output, not a property of code. It needs a different kind of check — sampling and evaluation, not an exact assertion — covered later in this phase.

contentSections.synthesis: Four of the six steps are ordinary software with no more randomness than a currency converter. Only one step — the model call itself — is genuinely non-deterministic, and a second — whether the output is *good* — is a judgment question rather than a code-correctness question. Everything else can and should have real, boring, deterministic unit tests, using a fixed stand-in response instead of a live API call. The next module covers exactly how to build that stand-in.

contentSections.body: In a typical AI-powered tool, one step is non-deterministic. The other four or five are ordinary code, and deserve ordinary tests.

contentSections.title: Temperature zero isn't a promise

contentSections.body: A developer sets `temperature: 0`, expecting the API to now return byte-identical output for byte-identical input every time — the way a pure function would. They write an exact-match test against it. It passes for two weeks, then fails on a Tuesday with no code changes anywhere.

contentSections.scenario: Same prompt, same `temperature: 0`, same model version string. The response was identical on every run for two weeks. Then, with no deploy and no config change, one run produces a response that differs by a single word from all the previous ones.
contentSections.question: What's the most likely explanation?

options.label: Temperature 0 doesn't actually guarantee bit-identical output — batching, routing, and infrastructure-level nondeterminism can still cause small variation
Someone on the team changed the prompt template without telling anyone
The API silently updated the model version behind the same model string

feedback.prompt: Worth checking, and it happens — but it's a code change you'd find in the diff. This scenario says no code changed, so it doesn't explain a variation appearing with the same inputs and the same deployed code.
feedback.silent: Providers do sometimes update what's behind a model identifier, and that's a real risk (covered in the next module). But it wouldn't typically show up as a single run differing from otherwise-identical runs over two weeks with everything else unchanged — that pattern points at something lower-level and intermittent.
feedback.infra: Right. Temperature 0 makes the model *strongly prefer* the highest-probability token at each step, which drastically reduces variation, but it does not make the underlying computation bit-identical run to run. Floating-point operations can execute in a different order depending on how requests get batched together on the serving infrastructure, and that can occasionally tip a near-tied probability the other way. It's rare, but it's real, and it means "deterministic" here is a strong tendency, not a guarantee.

contentSections.mechanism: **"Deterministic" is a spectrum here, not a binary switch.** Temperature 0 sits at the reliable end of that spectrum, and it's the right setting for anything where you want minimal variation — but treating it as equivalent to a pure function in your test suite (exact match, no tolerance, no fallback) will eventually produce exactly this kind of rare, unexplainable-looking failure. The practical response isn't to panic about infrastructure — it's to not build an assertion whose only path to passing is byte-identical text, even at temperature 0.

contentSections.body: This matters for how you write assertions, not just for how surprised you'll be in six months. At temperature 0, on short, constrained outputs (a classification label, a yes/no, a single extracted number), exact-match assertions are usually fine in practice — the space of possible answers is small enough that the rare infrastructure-level variation won't show up. On anything that produces free text of more than a few words, even at temperature 0, build the same habit from lesson one: assert the properties that have to be true, not the exact string. The failure mode isn't hypothetical — it's the one this lesson opened with.
Temperature 0 makes variation rare, not impossible — treat it as a strong tendency you can lean on for short, constrained outputs, not a guarantee that licenses exact-match assertions on free text.

title: Testing the plumbing separately from the model's judgment
description: Diagnosing a bug that looks AI-related but isn't, and writing real deterministic unit tests for the pipeline around the model call using a fixed stand-in response.

learningObjectives.text: Diagnose whether a bug lives in the model's output or in surrounding code
Write a deterministic unit test for pipeline code using a fixed stand-in for the model's response

contentSections.title: Two days on the prompt, for a CSV bug

contentSections.body: An expense-categorizer CLI reads receipts, calls Claude to assign a spending category, and writes rows to a CSV for the finance team. Finance reports that categories look shuffled — the amount from one receipt shows up next to another receipt's vendor. The team spends two days rewording the categorization prompt, certain the model is confusing receipts. The prompt changes make no difference, because the model was never the problem.

contentSections.scenario: The categorizer correctly identifies each receipt's vendor, amount, and category — verified by printing the model's raw response to the console, which is correct every time. The final CSV file still has vendors and amounts from different receipts on the same row.
contentSections.question: Where does two days of prompt tweaking waste look for the bug, and where does it actually live?

options.label: The model is occasionally confusing which receipt it's looking at — needs a clearer prompt
The CSV-writing code — likely writing columns in the wrong order or from a stale variable
The receipts are being uploaded in a corrupted order

feedback.model: This is where the team spent two days, and it's the least likely explanation given what's already been verified: the model's own response, printed straight from the API, is correct every single time. If the model were confusing receipts, that confusion would show up in the raw response — and it doesn't.
feedback.csv: Right. The model's output was confirmed correct before it ever reaches the CSV writer, which means the bug is downstream of the model entirely — ordinary code taking correct, structured data and writing it into the wrong place. A column-order mismatch or a loop variable that's captured by reference instead of by value are both classic, boring causes of exactly this symptom, and neither has anything to do with AI.
feedback.upload: Possible in principle, but it doesn't fit the evidence given: the model's response for each individual receipt is correct, which means each receipt was processed correctly on its own. The mismatch is happening after that, when results get assembled into rows.

contentSections.mechanism: **When the model's own output is already confirmed correct, the model stops being a suspect.** This sounds obvious written down and is exactly the step the team skipped under pressure — reworking a prompt is the reflex when anything about an AI-powered tool misbehaves, because the AI is the newest, least-familiar part of the system. But a mismatched CSV row is a data-plumbing bug wearing an AI costume. The fastest diagnostic step, always, is checking whether the model's raw response was correct *before* touching the prompt — it would have saved two days here.

contentSections.body: This is the direct payoff of separating the pipeline the way lesson two did. If you have real tests on the plumbing — the CSV writer, the request builder, the response parser — each with a fixed, known-good stand-in for what the model would return, a bug like this shows up immediately as a failing plumbing test with nothing about the model involved. Without that separation, every bug looks like it might be the model's fault, because the model is the one part of the system nobody fully controls, and it becomes the default place to look — which is exactly backwards, since it's usually the one part that's already working.
Once the model's raw output is confirmed correct, every bug downstream of it is an ordinary code bug — stop suspecting the prompt.

contentSections.title: Writing the plumbing test that catches it

contentSections.body: Splitting a pipeline into plumbing and judgment is a diagnosis tool after the fact. Used earlier, as a testing habit, it prevents the two-day detour from happening at all — because the CSV writer gets its own test, against a fixed input, with no API call anywhere near it.

contentSections.problem: Write a test for the expense categorizer's CSV-writing function, `writeExpenseRow(parsedResult, csvWriter)`, where `parsedResult` is the already-parsed, typed object the model's response gets turned into: `{ vendor: string, amount: number, category: string }`.

steps.label: Build a fixed stand-in for the model's output
steps.work:
`const fixedResult = { vendor: 'Staples', amount: 42.17, category: 'Office Supplies' };`

This is not a real API response — it's a plain object, written by hand, standing in for what the parser would have produced from a real one.
steps.why: No API call, no non-determinism, no network flakiness or cost. The test's job is to check the CSV writer, not to check the model, so the model is entirely absent from it.

steps.label: Call the function under test with that fixed input
steps.why: This is where the real question of the test gets asked: given correct, known input, does the plumbing do the right thing with it?

steps.label: Assert the exact output — this time, exact-match is correct
steps.why: Exact-match assertions are the wrong tool against a model's free text, but they're exactly the right tool here, because the input is fixed and the function is ordinary deterministic code. This is the whole point of the separation: it lets you keep using the testing techniques you already know, on the parts of the tool where they still apply.

steps.label: Add a second fixture that would have caught the real bug
steps.work:
`const secondResult = { vendor: 'Acme Corp', amount: 9.99, category: 'Software' };`
Run both through the writer in sequence and assert each row independently, checking that row two's vendor doesn't leak into row one or vice versa.
steps.why: The original bug was a mismatch *between* rows — one receipt's amount next to another's vendor — which a single-fixture test can miss if the bug only appears when processing more than one item in sequence, e.g. from a loop variable captured by reference.

faded.problem: Now write the equivalent test for the request-builder function, `buildCategorizationRequest(receipt)`, which takes a parsed receipt `{ vendorGuess: string, rawText: string }` and returns the request object sent to the API.

blanks.prompt: What goes into the test's input — a real receipt image, or something else?
blanks.why: Same principle as step one: the test's job is the request builder, not receipt parsing or the model, so the input should be a plain fixed object with known values.

blanks.prompt: Should the assertion check exact equality of the built request object, or something looser?
blanks.why: Request-building is ordinary string/object assembly from known data — no model involved yet, no reason to loosen the assertion.

blanks.prompt: Name one bug this test would catch that has nothing to do with the model's judgment.
blanks.answer: a typo in a template variable name / a missing field in the built request
blanks.why: This is exactly the class of bug that gets wrongly blamed on the model — a template that silently drops or mis-inserts a field produces a bad request regardless of how good the model is at its actual job.

contentSections.procedure: **Fixed stand-in in → assert exactly what should come out, with no API call anywhere in the test.** Apply this to every step of the pipeline that doesn't require the model to decide anything, and the two-day-CSV-bug never happens, because the CSV writer would have had a failing test the moment the mismatch bug was introduced.

contentSections.body: A plumbing test uses a fixed stand-in for the model's output and asserts exactly — no API call, no loosened assertion, because nothing non-deterministic is anywhere near it.

title: Flaky-by-design versus flaky-by-bug
description: Why silent retries destroy the evidence needed to tell harmless variation from a real, input-triggered defect — and how to read a failure pattern to tell them apart.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why unlogged retries mask real regressions
Distinguish flaky-by-design from flaky-by-bug from a pattern of failures

contentSections.title: The retry that hides the regression

contentSections.body: A CI run fails one test in twenty on the same commit, no code changes. The team's standing fix is a retry wrapper: run the test up to three times, pass if any attempt succeeds, log nothing about the failures. Suite stays green. Three weeks later, a prompt change ships that makes the categorizer wrong on refund-related tickets about 15% of the time — and the retry wrapper quietly passes it, because 85% of attempts still succeed within three tries.

contentSections.question: What's the actual defect in this retry pattern, beyond "it hides flakiness"?

options.label: It never logs what the failing attempts actually returned before they were discarded
Three attempts is too few — it should retry ten times
It should use exponential backoff between attempts

feedback.toofew: More retries makes the symptom (an intermittent failure disappearing) even more likely to be masked, not less — it moves further from the real fix, not toward it.
feedback.backoff: Backoff is a reasonable pattern for retrying genuinely transient issues like rate limits, but it doesn't address the actual problem here, which is that failures vanish with zero record of what they were.
feedback.nolog: Right. The wrapper discards every piece of information about what went wrong on the failing attempts — what the model actually returned, what the assertion expected, how often this test needed a retry at all. Without that, there's no way to ever notice that a test's failure rate has changed from one-in-twenty to one-in-seven, which is exactly the shape a real regression takes when it doesn't break something outright but makes it wrong more often.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A blanket retry-and-forget turns every test failure into silence. The fix isn't to stop retrying — some failures genuinely are transient network or rate-limit blips, and retrying those is reasonable — it's to log every failed attempt's actual output before discarding it, and to track failure *rate* over time rather than just pass/fail on the final attempt. A test that used to need a retry once a month and now needs one on every third run is telling you something, and a silent retry wrapper is specifically built to make sure nobody ever finds out.

contentSections.body: The distinction this lesson turns on: **flaky-by-design** is variation that's expected and harmless — a rate-limit blip, a network hiccup, the rare infrastructure-level nondeterminism from lesson two. **Flaky-by-bug** is variation that looks the same from the outside — an intermittent test failure — but is actually a real defect that only shows up on certain inputs: a prompt that's ambiguous on refund-adjacent tickets specifically, a parsing edge case that only trips on a particular JSON shape. Both produce the same CI symptom. They need completely different responses, and a retry wrapper with no logging makes it impossible to tell them apart.
A retry that discards the failing attempt's output doesn't fix flakiness — it deletes the evidence that would tell you whether the flakiness is a bug.

contentSections.title: Reading the cluster

contentSections.body: Once failures are actually logged instead of discarded, the question becomes: how do you tell flaky-by-design from flaky-by-bug apart, looking at a week of CI history?

contentSections.scenario: A team turns on failure logging (no more silent retries) and reviews two weeks of test failures for the categorizer's test suite.
contentSections.question: Select every signal below that points toward flaky-by-bug rather than flaky-by-design.

items.label: Failures cluster heavily on tickets tagged 'refund' — 40% of refund-ticket tests fail at least once, versus 2% of others
Failures are evenly spread across every ticket type at roughly the same low rate
Failures happen more often during a specific hour that correlates with a known provider maintenance window
Every logged failure on refund tickets shows the same specific wrong category being assigned
The specific wrong output differs every time, with no discernible pattern

explanation.cluster: A failure rate that's dramatically higher on one specific category of input, rather than spread evenly, is the signature of a real defect that particular inputs trigger — not random noise, which wouldn't care what the ticket was about.
explanation.spread: An even, low background rate across everything is closer to what infrastructure-level noise looks like — nothing about the content of any particular input makes it more likely to fail.
explanation.timeof: A time correlation with a known external event (a maintenance window, a rate-limit reset boundary) points at infrastructure, not a content-triggered bug — this is exactly the kind of pattern that's fine to retry past, as long as it's logged and tracked.
explanation.sameoutput: Consistency in *what* the wrong answer is — not just that it's wrong, but that it's the same specific wrong answer repeatedly — is strong evidence of a systematic issue (a prompt that's genuinely ambiguous for this case) rather than random variation.
explanation.random: If the wrong output is different every time with no pattern, that's closer to what you'd expect from noise near a genuine decision boundary, rather than a specific defect steering things toward one wrong answer.

contentSections.synthesis: The tell, across all of these, is **whether the failure correlates with something about the input's content** (a ticket category, a specific wrong answer repeating) versus something external to it (time of day, an infrastructure event, an even spread with no pattern). The first kind is a bug hiding behind the word "flaky." The second kind is the ordinary cost of depending on a network service, and retrying it — with logging — is the right call.

contentSections.body: The practical rule this leaves you with: **log every failure with its actual output before any retry happens, and periodically check whether failures cluster by input type.** A test that fails 1-in-20 with no pattern and clears on retry is probably fine to retry. A test that fails 1-in-20 and every one of those failures is on the same category of input is not flaky — it's a bug that hasn't been given a large enough sample to get caught yet, and the retry wrapper is actively working to keep it that way.
Flaky-by-design spreads evenly and correlates with external events. Flaky-by-bug clusters on specific inputs and often repeats the same wrong answer — check the pattern before you retry past it.

title: Deciding what actually needs a test here
description: Matching testing effort to a component's actual cost of being wrong — not to how AI-involved it is or how easy it is to write an assertion for.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate whether a component's testing effort matches what it costs when wrong
Justify leaving a low-stakes behavior untested and monitored instead

contentSections.title: You can't test every phrasing

contentSections.body: A team tries to build "complete" test coverage for a customer-facing chatbot by writing an assertion for every way a user might ask a question. After three weeks and 400 test cases, new phrasings still get through untested, the suite takes eleven minutes to run, and half the team has quietly stopped trusting it.

contentSections.scenario: The chatbot handles four kinds of requests. Here's what each one needs, and what it's currently getting.
contentSections.question: Select every situation below where the testing effort is mismatched to what the request actually needs — either badly over- or under-tested.

items.label: Answering FAQ-style questions from a fixed knowledge base — has 200 exact-phrasing test cases
Approving refunds up to $500 automatically — has 3 test cases, all happy-path
Responding to greetings and small talk — has 40 test cases checking exact wording
Deciding when to hand off to a human agent — has a sampled set of 30 real transcripts reviewed for correct escalation

explanation.faq: 200 exact-phrasing cases for a bounded, low-stakes lookup task is far more effort than the task needs — this is a case for a handful of representative phrasings plus a check that the answer is grounded in the actual knowledge base, not hundreds of near-duplicate string assertions.
explanation.refund: This is the inversion of the FAQ problem and the more dangerous one: an action that moves real money, tested only on the easy case. This deserves the deepest testing in the whole tool — edge cases, adversarial inputs, boundary amounts — and it's getting the least.
explanation.smalltalk: Exact-wording tests on "hi, how can I help you today" variations spend real engineering time on the lowest-stakes surface in the entire tool. Getting a greeting slightly wrong costs approximately nothing.
explanation.escalate: This is the well-matched one: a judgment call (does this conversation need a human) tested by sampling real examples and checking the decisions, rather than either an exhaustive phrasing list or no testing at all.

contentSections.synthesis: The pattern across the three mismatched cases is the same: effort was allocated by what was *easy to write tests for*, not by what the task actually needs. Exact-phrasing tests are easy to write and cheap to run, so they proliferated on the low-stakes, bounded tasks where they barely matter. The refund approval — the one thing in this tool that can cost real money if it's wrong — is exactly the case that needed the deepest testing and got the shallowest, because deep testing of a judgment call is harder to write than another exact-match string check.

contentSections.body: A more honest framework: for every component, ask what it would actually cost if it's wrong, and how likely it is to be wrong in a way testing could catch. Deterministic plumbing (from lesson two) gets thorough, ordinary tests — it's cheap and the payoff is real. The model's judgment on bounded, low-stakes tasks (FAQ answers, small talk) gets a handful of representative samples, not exhaustive phrasing coverage — the cost of occasionally being slightly off is close to zero. The model's judgment on high-stakes actions (approving a refund, sending an email, modifying a record) gets the most testing effort of anything in the tool, including edge cases and adversarial inputs — covered in the next two modules. And some low-stakes behavior is deliberately **not tested at all**, monitored in production instead, when the cost of building a test exceeds the cost of an occasional bad output.
Match testing effort to what a component actually costs when it's wrong, not to how easy it is to write an assertion for.

contentSections.title: The matrix that decides it

contentSections.body: A marketing-copy drafting tool and a refund-approval tool sit in the same codebase, built by the same team, in the same sprint. One of them deserves a test plan with edge cases and adversarial inputs. The other deserves a handful of examples and a human always reviewing before anything ships.

contentSections.scenario:
Two features, same team, same week:

**Feature A:** drafts three headline options for a blog post. A human always reviews and picks one before anything is published.

**Feature B:** decides whether to auto-approve a customer refund up to $500, no human review, money moves immediately on approval.
contentSections.question: Which one needs the deeper testing investment, and why?

options.label: Feature A — headline quality directly affects readership and revenue
Feature B — it acts autonomously on something costly and irreversible
Both equally — any AI-generated output needs the same rigor

feedback.a: Headline quality matters commercially, but a bad headline suggestion costs almost nothing, because a human is in the loop and simply won't pick it. The human review is itself a safety net that testing doesn't need to duplicate.
feedback.b: Right. The refund approval acts without a human checking it, and a wrong decision moves real money that may not be easy to claw back. That combination — autonomous action, real cost, hard to reverse — is exactly what should route the most testing budget in the codebase, including the edge-case and adversarial-input work covered in modules four and five of this phase.
feedback.equal: Treating every AI-generated output as equally deserving of test rigor is how a team ends up spending three weeks on chatbot small talk (as in the first half of this lesson) while a refund approver ships with three happy-path tests. The whole point of this lesson is that they're not equal.

contentSections.concept: **Blast radius, not AI-ness, decides testing depth.** The relevant question for any component isn't "does this call the model" — it's "if this is wrong, who finds out, how, and what does it cost to undo." A wrong headline suggestion is caught by the human right there in the workflow and costs a moment's annoyance. A wrong refund approval is discovered by finance days later, if at all, and costs real money. Two components that look structurally identical — both call the model, both parse a response, both act on it — can need completely different testing investments once you ask what happens when each one is wrong.

contentSections.body: This is what the lab in this module asks you to do concretely: pick one real AI-powered feature and write a test plan that states, for each piece of it, what gets asserted deterministically (the plumbing), what gets sampled and checked for a property rather than an exact match (bounded judgment calls), and — explicitly — what's being left untested and monitored in production instead, with a stated reason. That last category isn't a gap in the plan. Saying "we're not testing this, and here's why that's an acceptable choice given what it costs to be wrong" is a real, defensible engineering decision, and an honest test plan says so instead of pretending everything got equal coverage.
Ask what a component costs when it's wrong and how likely testing is to catch that, before deciding how much testing effort it deserves — not whether it happens to involve the model.

title: Practice — Classify seven AI-tool components by what to test
