contentSections.title: Seven drills

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Seven drills across the module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Do them in one sitting or split across days — nothing is timed and the set doesn't expire.
If a drill needed a hint, that's the thing to revisit at the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Write a test plan for one AI-powered feature
description: Produce a real test plan for an AI-powered feature: what's asserted deterministically, what's sampled, and what's deliberately left untested and why.

learningObjectives.text: Classify every step of a real feature's pipeline as plumbing or judgment
Produce a test plan matching testing depth to each step's actual stakes

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Every AI-powered feature that ships without a test plan gets one eventually — usually written the week after something like the invented refund policy reaches a customer. Writing it first, deliberately, while nothing is on fire, is the entire point of this lab.

contentSections.title: Write a test plan for one AI-powered feature
contentSections.brief:
Pick one real or realistic AI-powered feature — from a tool you're building, have built, or are planning. It should have at least one step where the model makes a genuine judgment call, not just a single trivial API call.

Write a test plan for it: not the tests themselves, but the document that says what gets tested, how, and what's deliberately left untested and why.
contentSections.deliverable: A test plan naming what's asserted deterministically and what's sampled — plus what's deliberately untested and monitored instead, with a stated reason.

stages.title: Map the pipeline
stages.instructions: List every step your feature takes from input to final effect (the way lesson two split the summarizer into six steps). For each step, mark it as deterministic plumbing or the model's judgment. If a step mixes both — e.g., a function that both calls the model and does something deterministic with the result — split it into two steps.
stages.checkpoint: Every step in your pipeline is marked plumbing or judgment, with nothing left unmarked.

stages.title: Decide what's asserted vs. sampled vs. skipped
stages.instructions: For each plumbing step, say what a fixed-input, exact-match test would check (lesson three's pattern). For each judgment step, decide: is this bounded and low-stakes enough for a small representative sample checked for a property (lesson five), or high-stakes enough to need deeper, adversarial testing? Name at least one component you're deliberately leaving untested and monitored in production, with a real reason tied to its cost of being wrong.
stages.checkpoint: Every step from stage one has a testing decision attached, including the untested one, each with a stated reason.

stages.title: Write the plan and self-check
stages.instructions: Write it up as a real document someone else on your team could follow: pipeline map, testing decision per step, and the flaky-by-design-vs-bug policy you'd use for this feature's CI (what gets logged, what triggers a retry, what doesn't). Then run the self-check below against your own draft.
stages.checkpoint: The document is something a teammate could pick up and start implementing tests from, without needing to ask you what you meant.

rubric.criterion: Every pipeline step is classified
rubric.meets: No step is left unmarked as plumbing or judgment; mixed steps are split rather than left ambiguous.

rubric.criterion: Plumbing tests specify a fixed stand-in, not a real API call
rubric.meets: Each plumbing testing decision names the fixed input it would use and an exact-match assertion, with no live API dependency.

rubric.criterion: Judgment tests are sampled, not exhaustively phrased
rubric.meets: No judgment step is tested by an exhaustive list of exact phrasings — sampling and property checks are used instead.

rubric.criterion: At least one component is deliberately untested with a real reason
rubric.meets: The untested item's reason is about its actual low cost of being wrong, not about it being hard to test.

rubric.criterion: High-stakes judgment gets proportionally more testing depth
rubric.meets: If the feature has any high-stakes, autonomous action, its testing plan is visibly deeper than the plan for low-stakes pieces.

rubric.criterion: States a flaky-by-design vs. flaky-by-bug policy
rubric.meets: Names what gets logged before a retry and what pattern would upgrade a 'flaky' failure to a real bug investigation.

contentSections.body: A test plan written before anything ships is a design document. Written after an incident, it's a post-mortem. Same content, very different cost.

title: Checkpoint — Why AI Tools Need Different Testing
description: Ten questions across the module. Ungraded, untimed — getting one wrong just means it comes back later.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve the module's core distinctions without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Why AI Tools Need Different Testing

questions.from: This module — Why AI Tools Need Different Testing
questions.prompt: Why is asserting exact output text usually the wrong check for a generative model call?

options.label: Because the same correct answer can be phrased differently each run
Because the API is too slow to test
Because generative calls never produce the same meaning twice

questions.explanation: The model can express the same correct meaning in different words from run to run, which exact-match assertions treat as a failure even though nothing is actually wrong. Option c overstates it — the meaning is often stable even when the wording isn't.

questions.from: This module — Why AI Tools Need Different Testing
questions.prompt: What's wrong with changing a failing assertion to `output.length > 0`?

options.label: It's too strict
It passes for almost any output, including a wrong one, so it stops checking anything meaningful
It requires a real API call

questions.explanation: A near-vacuous assertion goes green for outputs that are completely wrong, which is worse than having no test, because it creates false confidence.

questions.from: This module — Why AI Tools Need Different Testing
questions.prompt: In a typical AI-powered tool's pipeline, how many steps are usually genuinely non-deterministic?

options.label: All of them, since the model is involved somewhere
Usually just the model call itself — the rest is ordinary code
None, if temperature is set to 0

questions.explanation: Validation, request-building, response-parsing, and storage are ordinary deterministic code even in a tool that calls a model — only the generation step itself is genuinely non-deterministic.

questions.from: This module — Why AI Tools Need Different Testing
questions.prompt: Does temperature 0 guarantee byte-identical output across runs?

options.label: Yes, always
No — it strongly reduces variation but infrastructure-level effects can still cause rare differences
No, temperature 0 has no effect on consistency at all

questions.explanation: Temperature 0 makes variation rare, not impossible — batching and floating-point effects on the serving side can still produce occasional differences.

questions.from: This module — Why AI Tools Need Different Testing
questions.prompt: A CSV bug turns out to be a column-order mistake in code that runs after a model call whose raw output was already confirmed correct. What does this demonstrate?

options.label: The model needs a clearer prompt
Once the model's raw output is confirmed correct, the bug is in the surrounding code, not the model
The bug is unfixable without more training data

questions.explanation: A confirmed-correct raw model response rules the model out as the cause — the bug has to be downstream, in ordinary deterministic code.

questions.from: This module — Why AI Tools Need Different Testing
questions.prompt: What should a plumbing-layer test use as input instead of a live API call?

options.label: A fixed, hand-written stand-in for what the model's response would look like
A real API call with retries enabled
The average of several past real responses

questions.explanation: A fixed stand-in makes the test fast, free, and fully deterministic, since the plumbing code's correctness doesn't depend on the model at all.

questions.from: This module — Why AI Tools Need Different Testing
questions.prompt: What's the key problem with a retry wrapper that silently discards failed attempts' output?

options.label: It makes the suite slower
It destroys the evidence needed to tell a harmless blip from a real, worsening bug
It costs more in API calls than it's worth

questions.explanation: Without logging what a failed attempt actually returned, there's no way to notice a rising failure rate or a pattern that would reveal a real defect.

questions.from: This module — Why AI Tools Need Different Testing
questions.prompt: Which pattern points toward flaky-by-bug rather than flaky-by-design?

options.label: Failures spread evenly across all input types at a low rate
Failures cluster on one input category and repeat the same wrong answer
Failures correlate with a known provider maintenance window

questions.explanation: Clustering by input content, especially with a repeating specific wrong answer, is the signature of a real, input-triggered defect rather than random noise.

questions.from: This module — Why AI Tools Need Different Testing
questions.prompt: What should decide how much testing effort a component gets — how AI-involved it is, or something else?

options.label: How AI-involved it is — any model call deserves maximum scrutiny
What it costs when it's wrong and how likely testing is to catch that
How easy it is to write an assertion for

questions.explanation: Blast radius — real-world cost of a wrong outcome — should drive testing depth, not how novel or AI-adjacent a component feels.

questions.from: This module — Why AI Tools Need Different Testing
questions.prompt: Is it ever a defensible choice to leave part of a feature deliberately untested?

options.label: No, everything must have a test to be responsible engineering
Yes, when the cost of being wrong is low enough that monitoring in production is a reasonable substitute, and the reason is stated
Yes, but only for features nobody will ever notice

questions.explanation: Leaving something untested with a stated, real reason tied to low cost-of-being-wrong is an honest engineering decision, not a gap — the dishonest version is leaving it untested silently, with no stated reason at all.

title: Why real API calls in tests are slow, costly and flaky
description: The concrete costs of testing against a live model call on every run, and what a mock actually replaces — and doesn't.

learningObjectives.text: Explain the cost of running live API calls in a CI-triggered test suite
Distinguish what a mocked test verifies from what it cannot

contentSections.title: Three hundred tests, one API bill

contentSections.body: A team's test suite for their document-tagging tool calls the real Claude API on every run — 40 tests, each making one call. CI runs on every push. By the end of the month the API bill for tests alone is larger than the bill for the actual product traffic, and a flaky network blip on a shared runner fails the build for a reason that has nothing to do with anyone's code.

contentSections.scenario: A developer pushes a one-line CSS fix to an unrelated part of the app. CI runs the full suite, including all 40 API-calling tests. One of them times out because the API had a slow minute. The build goes red. The developer re-runs CI, it passes the second time with no code changes.
contentSections.question: What did that red build actually tell the team?

options.label: That the CSS change broke something
Nothing about the code — it was a transient network condition unrelated to any change
That the model's behavior had shifted since the last run

feedback.css: The CSS change touched nothing that could plausibly cause an API timeout in an unrelated tagging test — the red build has no relationship to what was actually changed.
feedback.nothing: Right, and that's the expensive part. A build that fails for reasons unrelated to the change trains people to re-run CI instead of reading the failure, which is exactly how a real failure eventually gets re-run past instead of investigated.
feedback.model: A single slow response is far more likely to be an ordinary network or infrastructure blip than a change in model behavior — and even if it were the latter, a timeout wouldn't be how you'd find out.

contentSections.concept: **A test suite that depends on a live network call inherits every failure mode of that network call**, on every run, whether or not the change being tested has anything to do with it. Real API calls in tests are slow (network round-trips add up across dozens of tests), costly (every CI run on every push is real spend, multiplied by however many pushes a team makes in a day), and flaky (rate limits, timeouts, and transient errors fail builds for reasons unrelated to the code change that triggered them).

contentSections.body: None of this is an argument against ever calling the real API in a test — the last lesson of this module is specifically about when a real call earns its cost. It's an argument for making that a deliberate, rare choice rather than the default for all 40 tests. The default should be a **mock**: a stand-in for the API that returns a known, controlled response without making a network call at all. This is the direct continuation of last module's plumbing-versus-judgment split — mocking is *how* you get a fixed stand-in for what the model would return, instead of just asserting one exists.
A test suite that calls the real API on every run inherits the API's latency, cost, and flakiness on every run — a mock removes all three without weakening what gets checked.

contentSections.title: What a mock actually replaces

contentSections.body: "Mocking" sounds like it might mean faking the thing you're supposed to be testing. It doesn't — it means replacing the one genuinely non-deterministic dependency so the deterministic code around it can be tested honestly, the same distinction lesson three of the last module drew between plumbing and judgment.

contentSections.question: What does this test actually verify?

options.label: That the tagger correctly identifies document topics
That the code correctly passes through whatever the mock returns — nothing about real tagging accuracy
Nothing — mocking the call makes the test meaningless

feedback.topics: The mock always returns `['general']` regardless of what document goes in — the test can't be checking topic-identification accuracy, because the thing that decides topics (the model) has been replaced with a constant.
feedback.passthrough: Right. This test verifies that `tagDocument` correctly takes whatever the API layer returns and passes it through to the result — a real, useful thing to check, since a bug in that plumbing would break every document regardless of what the model said. It says nothing about whether the *tags themselves* would be accurate for a real document, because that question requires the real model, sampled and evaluated the way lesson five of the last module described, not a mock.
feedback.meaningless: The test isn't meaningless — it's answering a narrower, real question than "is the tagging accurate." The mistake would be treating this test as if it answered that broader question when it structurally cannot.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A mock replaces the model's judgment, not the code around it. This test is legitimate and useful for exactly what it checks — that the plumbing between the API layer and the final result works — and it is not, and was never going to be, evidence about tagging accuracy. Confusing the two is the mistake: seeing a green mocked test and concluding "tagging works" when what actually passed was "the pass-through code works." Both are worth knowing. They are not the same fact.

contentSections.body: This sets up the boundary the rest of the module works inside: a mock is a fixed, controlled stand-in for the API response, used to test everything *around* the model call — request construction, response parsing, error handling, downstream logic. It cannot tell you whether the model's actual judgment is good, and a test suite that's entirely mocked, with nothing checking real model behavior anywhere, has quietly stopped testing the one part of the tool that's hardest to get right. The next lesson covers building a mock from a real response; the module's later lessons cover exactly how much of the suite should stay mocked versus real.
A mock tests the code around the model call, honestly and thoroughly. It cannot and does not test whether the model's judgment is good — that needs a different, deliberate kind of check.

title: Recording a real response and replaying it
description: Building a mock from a genuine captured API response rather than a hand-typed guess, and the staleness risk that comes with any fixture never refreshed.

learningObjectives.text: Build a record-and-replay mock from a genuine API response
Explain why an unrefreshed fixture can hide a real integration bug

contentSections.title: Capture it once, replay it forever

contentSections.body: The most honest mock isn't hand-written from imagination — it's a real response, captured once from an actual API call, saved to a file, and replayed on every subsequent test run. The model's judgment shaped it; the test just stops paying for it every time.

contentSections.problem: Build a record-and-replay mock for the document tagger's `callClaudeForTags(document)` function.

steps.label: Make one real call and save the exact response
steps.work: Run the real function once against a representative test document, and save the full raw API response — not a summary of it, the actual JSON — to a fixture file: `fixtures/tag-response-invoice.json`.
steps.why: Saving the exact real response, not a hand-typed approximation of what you expect it to look like, means the fixture has the real shape: real field names, real nesting, any quirks of how the API actually formats things — which a hand-written guess would likely get subtly wrong.

steps.label: Build a replay function that reads the fixture instead of calling the API
steps.why: This function has the exact same signature and return shape as the real one, so it can be swapped in wherever the real function is called, with the rest of the code none the wiser.

steps.label: Swap it in via dependency injection, not by patching the module
steps.work: `tagDocument(doc, { callClaude: mockCallClaudeForTags })` rather than `tagDocument(doc)` reaching for a hardcoded import internally.
steps.why: Passing the function in as a parameter (or an injected dependency) means the test controls exactly what's used, with no global module-patching magic that can leak between tests or behave differently depending on import order.

steps.label: Write the assertion against the fixture's known shape
steps.work: `expect(result.tags).toEqual(['invoice', 'finance', 'q3-2026']);` — matching exactly what the saved fixture's tags were.
steps.why: Because the fixture is fixed and known, exact-match assertions are correct here, the same way they were correct against the fixed stand-in in the plumbing tests from the previous module.

faded.problem: Now do the same for a second scenario: a document the real model correctly refused to tag because it wasn't actually a supported document type (a blank page). Build the record-and-replay mock for that case.

blanks.prompt: What's the first step, in a few words?
blanks.answer: make one real call and save the response
accept: call the real api once and save it
blanks.why: Same principle regardless of the scenario — the refusal response should also come from a real call, not be invented, because a hand-written guess at what a refusal looks like will likely miss real details (an error code, a specific message format) that only a genuine response has.

blanks.prompt: What should the fixture filename convey?
blanks.answer: that this is the refusal/blank-document case
blanks.why: A fixture library that grows to dozens of files needs names that say what scenario each one captures, or it becomes unmanageable — this is a small habit that pays off directly the first time someone needs to find or update one.

blanks.prompt: Should the assertion in this test check for tags, or for something else?
blanks.answer: that no tags were assigned / that a refusal or empty result was returned
blanks.why: The point of this fixture is specifically the refusal path — the assertion should verify the tagger's code correctly surfaces that refusal, not silently treat it like a normal empty tag list.

contentSections.procedure: **Real call once, saved as a fixture, replayed forever, injected rather than patched.** Every fixture is a real response the model actually produced for a real scenario — which is what separates this from guessing at what a response might look like, a mistake that produces mocks that pass tests a real API response would fail.

contentSections.body: A fixture library built this way accumulates real, representative scenarios over time — the routine case, the edge case, the refusal, the malformed input — each one a genuine response the model actually gave once, not an invented approximation. That's worth more than it sounds: a hand-written mock response tends to be too clean, matching exactly what the developer expects rather than the sometimes-odd real shape the API actually returns, which can hide bugs that only show up against genuine responses.
Record a real response once, save it as a fixture, replay it forever — a captured real response catches shape quirks a hand-typed guess never will.

contentSections.title: The trap in a too-convenient fixture

contentSections.body: A fixture captured eight months ago still gets used today. In that time the API's response format gained an optional field, and the parsing code was updated to expect it. The old fixture doesn't have that field. The mocked test still passes — silently testing against a shape the real API stopped sending months ago.

contentSections.scenario: A parsing bug ships to production: the tagger crashes on a response that includes a new `confidence` field the API started returning last month. The mocked test suite is entirely green — every fixture-based test passes.
contentSections.question: Why didn't the mocked tests catch this?

options.label: The fixtures were captured before the API added the new field, so no test ever exercised the new shape
Mocked tests are fundamentally incapable of catching parsing bugs
The parsing code has no bugs — the crash is unrelated to fixtures

feedback.incapable: Mocked tests are exactly the right tool for catching a parsing bug — this one just never got the chance, because none of its fixtures contained the new field that triggers the crash.
feedback.unrelated: The crash is a parsing bug (the code doesn't handle a field it wasn't expecting), and it's directly related to fixture staleness — no fixture exercised that field, so no test exercised that code path.
feedback.stale: Right. A fixture captured once and never refreshed is a snapshot of the API's shape at that moment. If the real API's shape changes — a new field, a renamed one, a different nesting — and the fixture doesn't get updated, every test using it is now testing against a shape the real world has moved past, and will happily stay green while the actual integration breaks.

contentSections.mechanism: **A fixture is a snapshot, and snapshots go stale.** This is the specific risk of record-and-replay mocking, and it's the direct subject of the next lesson: mocked tests need a way to notice when the real API has drifted away from what the fixtures represent, or the suite's green checkmarks stop meaning what everyone assumes they mean.

contentSections.body: Nothing about this argues against fixture-based mocking — it argues for treating fixtures as something that needs periodic refreshing against the real API, not something captured once and trusted forever. A practical habit: re-capture core fixtures on a schedule (monthly, or whenever the API's changelog mentions a response-shape change), and keep the capture script around as a checked-in part of the repo rather than a one-off manual step someone ran two years ago and forgot.
A fixture is a snapshot of the API's shape at capture time — refresh it periodically, or a green mocked suite quietly stops meaning the real integration still works.

title: Mocking failure modes, not just the happy response
description: Why a fixture library built only from successful calls never tests how a tool handles the API failing, and how to choose which failure fixtures are actually worth building.

learningObjectives.text: Identify failure modes a happy-path-only fixture library never exercises
Construct failure-mode fixtures deliberately for a tool's actual usage pattern

contentSections.title: The suite that never sees a bad response

contentSections.body: A support-ticket triage tool's entire mocked test suite uses fixtures captured from successful, well-formed API responses. Every test is green. In production, the API returns a rate-limit error during a traffic spike, and the tool crashes with an unhandled exception, taking the whole request queue down with it — because nothing in the test suite had ever exercised what happens when the call fails.

contentSections.scenario: Here are eight things that can happen when calling the Claude API in production.
contentSections.question: Select every one of these that a test suite built only from happy-path fixtures would fail to exercise.

items.label: A well-formed, successful categorization response
A rate-limit error during a traffic spike
The request timing out entirely with no response
A response that's valid JSON but missing an expected field
The model declining to answer because the request violates its usage policies
A second well-formed successful response for a different document type
An authentication failure from an invalid or expired credential
A streamed response that gets cut off partway through

explanation.success: This is exactly what a happy-path-only fixture library does cover — which is precisely the problem, since it's the one category of response that was never going to break anything downstream.
explanation.ratelimit: A rate-limit response has a completely different shape and meaning than a successful one, and code that only ever saw success fixtures during testing has never been asked to handle it.
explanation.timeout: No response at all is a different failure entirely from a malformed one — the code needs to handle the absence of a response, which a fixture-only suite of real (even if broken) responses can't represent unless someone deliberately builds a timeout scenario.
explanation.malformed: A subtly broken response — valid JSON, wrong shape — is a very real production scenario (a provider-side bug, a version mismatch) that a suite of clean captured responses will never include unless someone injects it on purpose.
explanation.refusal: A policy refusal is a legitimate, common response type that looks structurally different from a normal categorization result, and code that doesn't expect it can easily mishandle it as if it were malformed or empty.
explanation.success2: Still happy-path — a second successful example doesn't add coverage of any failure mode, no matter how different the document type is.
explanation.authfail: An expired API key or credential rotation gone wrong is an operational reality that has nothing to do with model behavior and everything to do with whether the tool degrades gracefully or crashes.
explanation.partial: A connection dropping mid-stream is its own failure shape, distinct from both a clean success and a clean error — code has to know what to do with a response that's neither.

contentSections.synthesis: Six of the eight are failure modes, and a fixture library built only from successful calls exercises none of them. This isn't a gap you close by capturing more successful examples — it's a gap you close by **deliberately writing fixtures that represent failure**, on purpose, the same way a real API sometimes fails.

contentSections.body: Building a failure fixture doesn't require waiting for a real failure to happen and capturing it live — you can construct one deliberately, based on the API's documented error shapes (a rate-limit response has a known status code and error format; a malformed response is trivial to construct by hand precisely because you're not claiming it's a real captured example, you're claiming it's a plausible broken one). The goal of a failure-mode fixture isn't fidelity to a specific real incident — it's coverage of a category of thing that will eventually happen in production, tested before it does.
A fixture library built only from successful responses has never tested how the tool handles the API failing — and the API will fail, in production, on a day nobody's watching.

contentSections.title: Building the failure fixtures on purpose

contentSections.body: Once you know which failure modes matter for a given tool, building the fixtures for them is ordinary work — the harder part is deciding which ones are worth building, since not every tool needs every failure mode covered equally.

contentSections.intro: You're building the failure-mode fixture set for the ticket-triage tool. For each fixture, decide what it should represent and why it matters for this specific tool.

fields.prompt: A rate-limit fixture for a tool that processes tickets in a queue, one at a time, all day
options: Represents the API returning a 429 with a retry-after header — the tool should back off and retry, not crash or drop the ticket
Represents a successful response that happens to be slow
Not worth building — rate limits are rare
fields.correctValue: Represents the API returning a 429 with a retry-after header — the tool should back off and retry, not crash or drop the ticket

feedback.Represents the API returning a 429 with: Right — for a queue processing tickets continuously all day, hitting a rate limit eventually is close to certain, not a rare edge case, which makes this one of the highest-value failure fixtures to build.
feedback.Represents a successful response that ha: That's a latency scenario, not a rate-limit one — a genuine rate-limit response has a distinct shape (status code, retry-after header) that a slow success doesn't.
feedback.Not worth building — rate limits are rar: For a tool making continuous calls all day at volume, this is one of the more likely failure modes, not a rare one — worth building early, not skipped.

fields.prompt: A malformed-response fixture — valid JSON, but missing the `category` field the parser expects
options: Tests whether the parser fails gracefully (flags for manual review) rather than crashing or silently assigning a wrong category
Not useful since the API rarely sends malformed responses
Should be treated identically to a rate-limit error in the code
fields.correctValue: Tests whether the parser fails gracefully (flags for manual review) rather than crashing or silently assigning a wrong category

feedback.Tests whether the parser fails gracefull: Right — the two bad outcomes to guard against are a crash (worse than nothing) and a silent wrong default (worse still, since nobody notices). A graceful fallback to manual review is the third option this fixture should verify the code actually takes.
feedback.Not useful since the API rarely sends ma: Rare doesn't mean impossible, and a provider-side bug or an unexpected version mismatch can produce exactly this shape — the cost of testing it is low and the cost of mishandling it in production (a silently wrong ticket category) is real.
feedback.Should be treated identically to a rate-: The two need different handling — a rate limit is a signal to back off and retry the same request, while a malformed response usually means retrying won't help and a human needs to look at it.

fields.prompt: A policy-refusal fixture, for a ticket whose content happens to trip the model's own safety response
options: Tests that a refusal gets routed to a human queue with a clear reason, not treated as an empty or broken result
Not applicable to an internal support-ticket tool
Should cause the whole batch job to halt
fields.correctValue: Tests that a refusal gets routed to a human queue with a clear reason, not treated as an empty or broken result

feedback.Tests that a refusal gets routed to a hu: Right — a refusal is a legitimate response type, and the correct handling is routing it somewhere a human can look, with the reason preserved, rather than treating the shape as broken or silently dropping the ticket.
feedback.Not applicable to an internal support-ti: Any tool processing free-text user input, internal or external, can encounter content that trips a refusal — it's worth having a defined behavior for it rather than assuming it won't happen.
feedback.Should cause the whole batch job to halt: Halting an entire queue over one ticket's refusal would make a single edge case take down unrelated work — the right response is isolating and routing that one ticket, not stopping everything.

contentSections.synthesis: The fixtures worth building aren't chosen by imagining every conceivable failure — they're chosen by asking which failures are actually likely for *this* tool's usage pattern (a high-volume queue makes rate limits likely) and which ones would be expensive if mishandled (a silent wrong category is worse than a visible crash, which is worse than a graceful fallback). That's the same blast-radius reasoning from the previous module's last lesson, applied to failure modes instead of features.

contentSections.body: Build failure fixtures for the failures that are actually likely given how the tool is used, and expensive if mishandled — not an exhaustive list of every conceivable error shape.

title: Keeping a mock honest as the real API changes
description: Why an unrefreshed fixture library silently drifts from reality, and a scheduled, human-reviewed drift-check that keeps mocks honest without giving up their speed.

learningObjectives.text: Explain how API shape drift silently invalidates an unrefreshed fixture library
Design a scheduled process that detects fixture drift without reintroducing live-call cost to every test run

contentSections.title: The mock that lied for six weeks

contentSections.body: The API provider ships a change: a field that used to always be present in the response, `raw_confidence`, becomes optional and is now omitted for a subset of response types. Nobody on the team reads that changelog entry. Six weeks later, a production crash traces back to code that assumed the field would always be there — code the mocked test suite had approved the entire time, because every fixture still had the old, always-present field.

contentSections.scenario: A team has 30 fixtures in their mocking library, captured over the tool's first year, never refreshed since. The real API has shipped several response-shape changes in that time.
contentSections.question: Roughly what fraction of those 30 fixtures would you guess still exactly match what the real API returns for the same request today?
contentSections.actualValue: unpredictable, and that's the point — often far fewer than assumed
contentSections.explanation: There's no fixed number here worth memorizing — the real lesson is that nobody can answer this confidently without actually checking, and most teams don't check. A fixture doesn't announce that it's gone stale; it just sits there, syntactically valid, structurally plausible, quietly representing a version of the API that may not exist anymore. The only way to know is to periodically compare fixtures against fresh real responses — which is the concrete practice this lesson gets to.

contentSections.body: This is the same staleness risk from lesson two, now with a name for the mechanism: **a mock is only as honest as its last refresh.** The API a tool depends on is not a fixed target — providers add fields, deprecate others, occasionally change default behavior, and release new model versions behind the same identifier. None of that requires any code change on the tool's side to notice, which is exactly why it's easy to miss: nothing breaks until the day the drift finally collides with an assumption in the code, and by then the mocked suite has been giving a false all-clear for as long as the drift has existed.
A mock is only as honest as its last refresh — API shape drift doesn't announce itself, and a stale fixture keeps approving code that's quietly wrong.

contentSections.title: Keeping the mock honest without giving up mocking

contentSections.body: The answer isn't to stop mocking and go back to real calls everywhere — that reintroduces exactly the cost and flakiness this module opened with. The answer is a small number of real calls used specifically to police the mocks, on a schedule, separate from the main suite.

contentSections.question: Put these into the order that keeps a fixture library honest with the least ongoing cost.
steps: Keep the full mocked suite as the default for every CI run — fast, free, deterministic
On a schedule (weekly or monthly), run a small separate job that makes real calls for each core fixture scenario
Diff each real response's shape (field names and types) against the corresponding saved fixture
If a diff appears, open an alert or a PR rather than silently updating the fixture
A human reviews the diff, decides if it's a real shape change to accommodate, and updates the fixture deliberately
contentSections.explanation: The core move is separating two different jobs that used to be conflated: fast, cheap, deterministic testing (the mocked suite, run constantly) and slow, occasional honesty-checking (the drift-detection job, run rarely). Automatically overwriting the fixture the moment a diff appears would be a mistake — a shape change might indicate a real API update to accommodate, or it might indicate something worth investigating before quietly baking it in. A human reviewing the diff before it becomes the new fixture is what keeps this from turning into a different version of the same blind trust the stale fixture already demonstrated the risk of.

contentSections.body: This is a small, bounded cost — a handful of real calls on a schedule, not on every push — and it buys back almost all of the confidence a fully-live suite would provide, without the daily cost of one. It's also exactly the shape of answer the next lesson generalizes: a small number of deliberate real calls, chosen for what they specifically verify, rather than an all-or-nothing choice between real and mocked.
Keep the everyday suite fully mocked for speed and determinism, and add a small, scheduled, human-reviewed job whose only purpose is catching drift between fixtures and reality.

title: When a real call in CI is worth the cost
description: The narrow, deliberate case for real API calls in CI — checking live model judgment quality on a small, curated, scheduled basis, kept separate from the fast everyday mocked suite.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate competing positions on real-vs-mocked API calls in CI against the module's evidence
Size a real-call budget appropriately for checking judgment quality without reintroducing cost or flakiness

contentSections.title: The suite that's honest but never checks reality

contentSections.body: A team follows every rule in this module: fixtures captured from real responses, failure modes covered deliberately, a drift-check job running monthly. Their CI suite has made zero real API calls in eight months. It's fast, cheap, and it has never once verified that the actual, current, deployed model still produces reasonable output for the tool's real prompts.

contentSections.scenario:
Three positions on real API calls in CI, argued by three different engineers on the same team:

**A.** "Never call the real API in CI — it's slow, costly, and flaky. Mocking solves all of that."

**B.** "Always call the real API in CI — anything less isn't really testing the tool."

**C.** "Mock almost everything, but run a small, separate set of real calls on a schedule, checking output quality against a held-out set of real examples — not on every push."
contentSections.question: Which position best fits everything this module has covered so far?

options.label: A — mocking is strictly better once it's done well
B — anything mocked is not a real test
C — a small, deliberate, scheduled slice of real calls, separate from the fast everyday suite

feedback.a: This module's whole second half — failure fixtures, drift checks — exists because mocking alone, however well done, structurally cannot verify that the real model is still behaving well on real inputs. A mock can only ever be as good as its last capture; it can't tell you anything new about the live model.
feedback.b: This throws away everything the first three lessons established: cost, latency, and flakiness are real, and most of a tool's code (the plumbing) genuinely doesn't need a live call to test correctly.
feedback.c: Right, and it's the same shape of answer as lesson four's drift-check job — a small, deliberate, scheduled slice of real-world contact, kept separate from the fast everyday suite so it doesn't reintroduce the costs mocking was solving.

contentSections.concept: **Real calls in CI earn their cost when they're answering a question a mock structurally cannot answer** — specifically, whether the live model's actual judgment is still good, not whether the code around it works. That's a narrow, specific use, not a wholesale replacement for the mocked suite, and it doesn't need to run on every push to be valuable.

contentSections.body: What earns a real call: checking output *quality* against a small, curated, held-out set of real inputs with known-good expected properties — not exact answers, but the kind of property-based checks from the last module (does the categorization stay within the right topic, does the summary avoid inventing facts). This is different from — and is actually the seed of — the next module's territory: building a proper eval harness. For now, the practical rule is narrower: a small real-call job, on a schedule, checking a handful of representative cases, kept entirely separate from the mocked suite that runs on every push.
A real call in CI earns its cost by checking something a mock structurally can't — whether the live model's judgment is still good — not by re-testing the plumbing a mock already covers for free.

contentSections.title: Sizing the real-call budget

contentSections.body: "A small set, on a schedule" still needs a number. Too few real calls and drift in judgment quality goes unnoticed as long as shape drift did before lesson four. Too many and the cost problem from lesson one is back.

contentSections.scenario: A team is deciding what to include in their scheduled real-call job for the document tagger.
contentSections.question: Select every choice below that fits the narrow, deliberate use this lesson describes for real calls in CI.

items.label: A small, curated set of 10-15 representative real documents, covering the tool's main use cases
Running the full real-call set on every push, same as the mocked suite
Checking output properties (topic relevance, no invented facts) rather than exact string matches
Grabbing 500 random production documents each run for maximum coverage
Alerting a human if output quality on the held-out set drops, rather than failing the build silently and moving on

explanation.curated: Small and representative is exactly the right size for this job — enough to catch a real regression in judgment quality without reintroducing the cost problem the whole module opened with.
explanation.everypush: This reintroduces the exact cost and flakiness problem from lesson one for every single push, defeating the entire point of keeping the everyday suite mocked.
explanation.quality: Property-based checks are the right fit here, for the same reason exact-match assertions were wrong against free-text generative output back in the previous module.
explanation.random: 500 documents per run is expensive and mostly redundant — a well-chosen small set that deliberately covers the tool's known use cases and edge cases catches more real signal per dollar than a large random sample.
explanation.alert: Silent pass/fail on a judgment-quality check throws away the one thing this job exists to surface — a human needs to see what changed and decide whether it's a real regression, similar to how the drift-check job's diffs need human review rather than automatic action.

contentSections.synthesis: The size and shape of a real-call budget follows the same logic as everything else in this module: spend it where a mock structurally can't substitute, keep it small and deliberate rather than exhaustive, and route what it finds to a human rather than letting it pass or fail silently. That's a different job from the mocked suite, running on a different schedule, for a different reason — not a bigger version of the same thing.

contentSections.body: This closes the loop the module opened with: real API calls in tests are slow, costly, and flaky when they're the default for everything. They're none of those things, in proportion to what they buy, when they're a small, deliberate, scheduled check aimed specifically at the one question a mock can never answer. Getting that balance right — and building the harness that makes the quality check itself rigorous rather than a vibe-check — is where the next module of this phase picks up.
Size the real-call budget to be small, curated, property-checking, and human-reviewed — a different, narrower job than the everyday mocked suite, not a bigger version of it.

title: Lab — Add a mocked test suite to an AI-powered feature
description: Build a real, runnable mocked test suite with a captured success fixture, a deliberate failure fixture, and a concrete staleness-guard plan.

learningObjectives.text: Construct a mocked test suite from a captured response and a deliberate failure fixture
Produce a concrete plan for detecting fixture drift

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: This is where the module's four lessons become a real, checked-in test suite — not a plan this time, but working tests, mocked and real, for one actual AI-dependent feature.

contentSections.title: Add a mocked test suite to an AI-powered feature
contentSections.brief: Take one AI-powered feature — from your own project, or the test plan you wrote in the previous module's lab if it fits. Build a real, runnable mocked test suite for it: at least one success fixture, at least one deliberately-constructed failure fixture, and a documented plan for keeping it honest.
contentSections.deliverable: A suite that runs offline, including at least one mocked failure case.

stages.title: Capture and wire in a success fixture
stages.instructions: Make one real call for a representative input, save the raw response as a fixture, and build a replay function with the same signature as the real call. Wire it into your code via dependency injection, not module patching. Write at least one test against it using an appropriate assertion (exact-match for constrained output, property-based for free text, per the previous module).
stages.checkpoint: You have a captured (not hand-typed) fixture, a working replay function, and at least one passing test against it — all running with zero network calls.

stages.title: Construct a deliberate failure fixture
stages.instructions: Pick one failure mode that's actually likely for your feature's usage pattern (not just the first one you think of — use the likelihood-and-cost reasoning from lesson three). Build the fixture by hand, since you're not claiming it's a real capture, and write a test verifying your code handles it gracefully — no crash, no silent wrong behavior.
stages.checkpoint: You have a failure fixture your code has actually been tested against, with a passing test that would fail if the failure were mishandled.

stages.title: Write the staleness-guard plan
stages.instructions: You don't need to build the scheduled job for real in this lab — write down, concretely, what it would check (which fixtures, compared against what), how often it would run, and what would happen when it finds a diff (per lesson four: surfaced to a human, not auto-applied).
stages.checkpoint: The plan names specific fixtures, a specific cadence, and a specific human-review step — not a vague 'refresh periodically' statement.

stages.title: Run the suite and self-check
stages.instructions: Run your test suite and confirm it passes with zero network calls (disconnect from the internet if you want to prove it). Then run the self-check below against your own work.
stages.checkpoint: The suite runs green with no network access, and every check on the rubric below is genuinely met, not just plausible.

rubric.criterion: The success fixture is a real captured response
rubric.meets: The fixture file contains an actual response from a real API call, not a hand-typed approximation.

rubric.criterion: At least one failure fixture is deliberately constructed
rubric.meets: A failure fixture exists and is tied to a stated reason it's likely or costly for this specific feature.

rubric.criterion: Mocking uses dependency injection, not module patching
rubric.meets: The mock is swapped in as a passed-in function or injected dependency, not via global mocking magic.

rubric.criterion: Assertions match what's actually being tested
rubric.meets: Exact-match is used only where the underlying value is genuinely fixed; free-text output uses property checks.

rubric.criterion: The staleness-guard plan is concrete
rubric.meets: Names specific fixtures, a cadence, and a human-review step for handling detected drift.

rubric.criterion: The suite runs entirely offline
rubric.meets: Every test passes with zero live network calls, verified by actually checking, not assumed.

contentSections.body: A mocked suite that's fast, honest about failure modes, and has a real plan for staying current is worth more than a slower suite that calls the real API and trusts it blindly.
