fields.correctValue: Short — five specific yes/no questions, one per category from this module, not the full 40-item version

feedback.Short — five specific yes/no questions,: Right — a checklist embedded at the point of use needs to be scannable in under a minute, or people will skip past it the same way they'd skip past anything else that feels like a wall of text blocking their PR.
feedback.The full original 40-item document, past: A 40-item list inline in a PR template will get skimmed or skipped for the same reason the standalone document did — length that was fine for a reference document is too much friction for something meant to be checked every single time.
feedback.A single line: \"Remember to check edge: This has all the visibility problems solved and none of the content — it doesn't actually name what to check, so it relies entirely on the reader already remembering the five categories, which defeats the purpose of having a checklist at all.

fields.prompt: Should the checklist be optional or required to acknowledge before merging?
options: Required to check off, but genuinely fast to complete honestly — not a rubber-stamp gate that trains people to click through without reading
Fully optional, trusting engineers to consult it on their own judgment
Required, with the PR blocked from merging until every item is checked regardless of relevance
fields.correctValue: Required to check off, but genuinely fast to complete honestly — not a rubber-stamp gate that trains people to click through without reading

feedback.Required to check off, but genuinely fas: Right — required-but-fast is the balance that actually gets read rather than either ignored (fully optional) or rubber-stamped (a slow, rigid gate people learn to click through without thinking).
feedback.Fully optional, trusting engineers to co: This reintroduces exactly the 'requires remembering it exists' problem from the first half of the lesson — optional visibility at a workflow point is better than a buried document, but still relies on someone choosing to engage with it.
feedback.Required, with the PR blocked from mergi: A rigid, always-required-in-full gate on every PR regardless of whether it touches model input at all is exactly the kind of friction that trains people to check boxes without reading them — the goal is a fast, honest check, not a slow, mandatory ritual.

contentSections.synthesis: The plan that works is short, lives at a real workflow checkpoint every relevant change already passes through, and is required but fast enough that completing it honestly is easier than rubber-stamping it. None of that changes what the checklist actually contains — it changes whether the content this module built ever gets consulted at the moment it would matter.

contentSections.body: A checklist becomes real when it's short, lives at a workflow point every relevant change already passes through, and is fast enough to complete honestly — not when it's comprehensive but buried.

title: Practice — Find the edge case that breaks eight tools
description: Eight drills identifying which edge-case category — empty/huge/malformed input, format diversity, valid-but-wrong output, or adversarial content — breaks a given tool.

learningObjectives.text: Identify which edge-case category is most likely to break a given tool's specific design

contentSections.title: Eight drills

contentSections.body: Eight drills across the module's skills. Nothing new — this is where recognizing the five edge-case categories turns into finding the one that actually breaks a specific tool.
A drill that took a hint is worth another look at the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the whole set.

title: Lab — Edge-case test your tool and fix what breaks
description: Deliberately test a real tool against all four edge-case categories, fix what breaks without silent degradation, and produce a short, workflow-embedded checklist.

learningObjectives.text: Deliberately test a real tool against empty/huge/malformed, format-diversity, valid-but-wrong, and adversarial input categories
Produce a short, workflow-embedded edge-case checklist from real findings

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: The module's five categories, applied to one real tool, all the way through: find what breaks it, fix what's fixable, and leave behind the short checklist that keeps the next feature from repeating the same gaps.

contentSections.title: Edge-case test your tool and fix what breaks
contentSections.brief: Take one real AI-powered feature you're building or have built. Deliberately test it against each of this module's four failure categories, fix what you find, and produce the short, embeddable checklist this module's final lesson describes.
contentSections.deliverable: A checklist run against your tool with fixes for what it found.

stages.title: Test empty/huge/malformed and format diversity
stages.instructions: Deliberately try an empty input, an oversized input, and a malformed input against your tool. Then try at least one input from outside whatever language, date, or naming convention your tool was built around. Record what actually happens for each — not what you assumed would happen.
stages.checkpoint: You have real, observed results (not assumptions) for at least four deliberately-chosen edge inputs across these two categories.

stages.title: Test for valid-but-wrong output and adversarial input
stages.instructions: Construct at least one known-answer boundary case (per lesson three) and check whether your tool's output is not just valid but actually correct. Then try at least one adversarial input — either a direct instruction-shaped message, or content embedded inside a document if your tool processes documents.
stages.checkpoint: You have a known-answer case with a verified pass/fail result, and at least one adversarial input tested with its actual outcome recorded.

stages.title: Fix what broke, without silent degradation
stages.instructions: For each failure found, choose and implement reject, degrade visibly, or ask for clarification — explicitly avoiding silent degradation. If something can't be fixed in the time available, document it honestly as a known gap rather than leaving it silently unaddressed.
stages.checkpoint: Every discovered failure has either a real fix or an honestly documented, explicit gap — nothing is silently left as-is with no record.

stages.title: Write the short, embeddable checklist
stages.instructions: Write five specific yes/no questions — one per category from this module — sized to be read and honestly answered in under a minute, and say concretely where in your workflow (or your solo process) it would actually live.
stages.checkpoint: The checklist is five items or fewer, each one specific enough to actually check against a real feature, with a named real location for where it lives.

rubric.criterion: All four categories were actually tested, not assumed
rubric.meets: Each of empty/huge/malformed, format diversity, valid-but-wrong, and adversarial input has a real, observed test result.

rubric.criterion: At least one known-answer boundary case exists
rubric.meets: A specific input with a known correct output was tested, and the tool's actual output was checked against it exactly, not just for validity.

rubric.criterion: No fix relies on silent degradation
rubric.meets: Every fix either rejects cleanly, degrades with a visible signal, or asks for clarification — nothing silently returns a partial or wrong result unmarked.

rubric.criterion: Unfixed gaps are documented honestly
rubric.meets: Anything not fixed in the lab's time is explicitly named as a known gap, not silently dropped.

rubric.criterion: The checklist is short and specific
rubric.meets: Five items or fewer, each concrete enough to check against a real feature in under a minute.

rubric.criterion: The checklist has a real, named location
rubric.meets: States a specific workflow point (PR template, deploy script, pre-commit hook) rather than 'a document somewhere.'

contentSections.body: Finding an edge case that breaks your tool before a user does is worth more than the fix itself — it's evidence the checklist is catching real things, not just documenting hypothetical ones.

title: Checkpoint — Handling Edge Cases
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from Debugging Bad Output, two from further back. Ungraded, untimed.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve core distinctions from this module and earlier modules without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Handling Edge Cases

questions.from: This module — Handling Edge Cases
questions.prompt: Why is silent degradation (like truncating a document with no warning) more dangerous than a visible error?

options.label: Because the user has no way to know the result is incomplete and will likely trust it as complete
Because errors are always logged automatically
It isn't — silent degradation is always the safest default

questions.explanation: A silent partial result looks like a complete, trustworthy one, which is precisely what makes it more dangerous than an honest failure the user can see and act on.

questions.from: This module — Handling Edge Cases
questions.prompt: Why does a large but format-narrow test set still miss real bugs?

options.label: Because sample-size variety and format/convention variety are different axes, and more examples of one format don't add coverage of another
Because large test sets are always slower to run
Because format diversity doesn't actually affect model behavior

questions.explanation: 500 examples of one language and date convention still test only that convention — format diversity has to be deliberately included, not accumulated by adding more of the same kind of example.

questions.from: This module — Handling Edge Cases
questions.prompt: What's the difference between output validity and output correctness?

options.label: Validity checks whether output is well-formed; correctness checks whether it's actually right — schema checks can only ever verify the first
They're the same thing, checked by the same tools
Correctness is a subset of validity

questions.explanation: An off-by-one error or a wrong-but-allowed category can be perfectly valid (right shape, right type) while still being substantively wrong, which only a known-answer case can catch.

questions.from: This module — Handling Edge Cases
questions.prompt: Why is structural system/user channel separation a more durable defense than blocking specific adversarial phrases?

options.label: Because phrase-blocking is a losing game against endless rephrasing, while channel separation removes the mechanism regardless of wording
Because phrase-blocking is technically impossible to implement
Because channel separation blocks all adversarial content everywhere, including inside documents

questions.explanation: Channel separation doesn't rely on recognizing any specific wording, unlike a blocklist, which makes it durable against rephrasing — though it doesn't cover content-level manipulation smuggled inside documents, which needs its own defense.

questions.from: Previous module — Debugging Bad Output
questions.prompt: What are the three suspects for isolating a bad-output regression?

options.label: The prompt, the context, and the model
The frontend, the backend, and the database
The user, the developer, and the provider

questions.explanation: These three categories are what a regression should be isolated to before attempting a fix.

questions.from: Previous module — Debugging Bad Output
questions.prompt: Why is 'context' often the most-overlooked suspect in a bad-output regression?

options.label: Because it's assembled from outside data sources at request time and can drift without anyone editing the prompt or model config
Because context never actually affects output
Because it's technically the hardest to check

questions.explanation: Context drifts silently through data sources changing independently of the tool's own prompt and model configuration.

questions.from: Previous module — Debugging Bad Output
questions.prompt: What's wrong with a fix verified only against the exact case that was reported?

options.label: It's tested at a sample size of one and may have over-generalized, breaking other, previously-fine cases
Nothing — the original case is the only one that matters
It should instead be tested against every possible input exhaustively

questions.explanation: A fix can pass the reported case while over-correcting and breaking adjacent cases — a small near-neighbor set is needed to catch that.

questions.from: Previous module — Debugging Bad Output
questions.prompt: Why should the original failing case be run more than once before declaring a fix confirmed?

options.label: Because output variation means a single passing run could be luck rather than a reliably fixed behavior
Because a single run always takes too long
Because fixes should be tested by a different engineer

questions.explanation: A single run is one sample from a distribution that can vary, even at low temperature, so it can't distinguish a reliable fix from a lucky one.

questions.from: Module one — Why AI Tools Need Different Testing
questions.prompt: In a typical AI-powered tool's pipeline, how many steps are usually genuinely non-deterministic?

options.label: All of them
Usually just the model call itself — the rest is ordinary code
None, if temperature is 0

questions.explanation: Validation, request-building, parsing, and storage are ordinary deterministic code even in an AI-powered tool — only generation is genuinely non-deterministic.

questions.from: Module two — Mocking Claude in Tests
questions.prompt: Why is a fixture captured from a real API call more trustworthy than a hand-typed one?

options.label: It reflects the real shape and quirks of an actual response rather than a developer's guess
Captured fixtures are always shorter
Hand-typed fixtures are technically invalid JSON

questions.explanation: A real capture has whatever fields, nesting, and quirks the API actually produces, which a hand-written approximation is likely to miss.

title: A handful of real cases beats a vague sense it's fine
description: Why impressions from a few glanced-at examples aren't a measurement, and what a genuinely useful fixed eval case set actually requires.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why impression-based comparison fails to catch real regressions
Identify the properties a genuinely useful eval case set needs

contentSections.title: "It feels better" is not a measurement

contentSections.body: A team rewrites the prompt for their ticket-summarizer, certain the new version is an improvement — the summaries they skim look cleaner, more concise, more professional. They ship it. Support tickets about missed details triple within a week. Nobody had actually measured anything; the new version just *read* better on the handful of examples someone happened to glance at.

contentSections.scenario:
Two ways a team decides a prompt change is an improvement.

**A.** Three engineers read five example outputs from the old and new prompt side by side, and agree the new ones sound better.

**B.** The team runs both prompts against the same fixed set of 30 real support tickets with known-correct summaries, and counts how many summaries from each version correctly capture every action item.
contentSections.question: Which approach would have caught the tripled miss rate before shipping?

options.label: A — three engineers agreeing is a meaningful signal
B — a fixed set of real cases with a countable, checkable outcome
Neither — no pre-ship process can catch every issue

feedback.a: Three people's agreement about which output *reads* better is a judgment about style and fluency, not about whether the summary is actually capturing the right information — and "sounds more concise" is exactly the kind of quality that can come from *cutting* real content, which is precisely what happened here.
feedback.b: Right. A fixed set of real cases with a checkable outcome — did the summary include every actual action item — turns "feels better" into a number you can compare before and after. That's the only kind of check that would have surfaced a rise in missed details, because it's actually counting whether details got missed.
feedback.neither: No process catches everything, but that's a different claim from "nothing would have caught this specific, measurable regression" — a 30-case set checking action-item completeness is exactly targeted at the failure that happened, and very likely would have caught it before it shipped to real users.

contentSections.concept: **A handful of examples that "look better" to whoever's reading them is not evidence of anything except that those particular examples looked better to those particular readers.** It's the same single-sample trap this whole phase opened with — an assertion that passes once, a fix confirmed by one run — now showing up at the level of an entire prompt redesign. A real eval needs a fixed set of cases, a way to check the outcome that isn't just impression, and a comparison between versions on the same cases.

contentSections.body: This module is where the phase's threads converge. The earlier modules built the tools for testing individual pieces — plumbing tests, mocks, bug diagnosis, edge-case handling. An eval harness is the tool for the question none of those individually answer: **taken as a whole, on a real set of cases, is this feature actually good, and did the last change make it better or worse?** That's a different question from "does this pass" — it's "how well does this do, measured the same way, every time, so two versions can be honestly compared."
A handful of examples that look better to whoever glanced at them is not a measurement — an eval needs a fixed set of real cases and a checkable outcome, compared the same way across versions.

contentSections.title: What a real case actually needs

contentSections.body: "A fixed set of real cases" sounds simple until you try to build one — and the temptation is to grab whatever's convenient (the last ten support tickets in the queue) rather than building a set that actually represents what the feature needs to handle well.

contentSections.scenario: A team is building their first eval set for the ticket summarizer, and is considering what to include.
contentSections.question: Select every property below that a genuinely useful eval case set needs.

items.label: Each case has a known-correct or known-acceptable expected outcome, decided in advance
The set covers the range of real ticket types the tool actually handles, not just the easy ones
The exact same cases are used every time a comparison is run, not a fresh random sample each time
The cases are whatever's easiest to grab — the ten most recent tickets in the queue
It includes at least a few of the edge cases from the previous module — empty, ambiguous, or adversarial tickets
It needs to number in the thousands to be statistically meaningful

explanation.known: Without a predetermined expected outcome, there's nothing to check the actual output against — this is the same known-answer-case principle from the previous module's valid-but-wrong lesson, applied at the scale of a whole eval set.
explanation.representative: A set of only easy, obvious tickets will show every version looking great, and tell you nothing about the harder cases that actually differentiate a good summarizer from a mediocre one.
explanation.fixed: Using the exact same cases every run is what makes a before/after comparison honest — comparing version A's performance on one random sample to version B's performance on a different random sample conflates real improvement with sampling luck.
explanation.convenient: The most recent ten tickets are an accident of timing, not a deliberate representation of the tool's real range — likely to be skewed toward whatever happened to come in that week rather than the full range of cases the tool needs to handle.
explanation.edge: A small deliberate inclusion of the edge cases the previous module covered means the eval set also catches regressions in exactly the failure modes most likely to slip through — this is where the last two modules of this phase connect directly.
explanation.large: Statistical significance in the abstract-research sense isn't the goal here — a well-chosen 20-30 case set that's representative and has known answers catches most real regressions; a large but low-quality set of unlabeled or unrepresentative cases catches less, despite being bigger.

contentSections.synthesis: The properties that matter are known outcomes, real representativeness (including the hard and edge cases, not just the easy ones), and fixed repeatability across runs — not raw size and not convenience. A well-built 20-30 case set beats a large, thrown-together one on every dimension that actually matters for catching a regression before it ships.

contentSections.body: Building this set is real, deliberate work — closer to the labor of the previous module's edge-case testing than to something that assembles itself. A practical starting point: take 15-20 representative real cases spanning the tool's actual range of difficulty, hand-verify (or have a domain expert verify) the correct or acceptable outcome for each one, add 3-5 of the edge cases most likely to matter for this specific tool, and treat that set as a fixed, versioned asset — checked into the repo, not scattered across someone's notes — that every future prompt or model change gets run against before shipping.
A useful eval set needs known-correct outcomes, real representativeness across the tool's difficulty range including edge cases, and fixed repeatability — not raw size or convenience.

title: Scoring output automatically where you can
description: Why manual scoring gets skipped exactly when it's most needed, and how to build automated scoring for checkable properties without repeating the exact-match mistake on free text.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why automated scoring is necessary for an eval to survive real deadline pressure
Design an appropriate automated scoring method for a given output type

contentSections.title: Scoring what a computer can actually check

contentSections.body: Having a fixed eval set with known answers doesn't automatically mean scoring it is free — someone still has to compare each output against its expected answer, and for a set that's checked on every change, doing that by hand every time defeats the purpose.

contentSections.scenario: A team has a 25-case eval set for their invoice-categorizer, with a known-correct category for each invoice. Every time they tweak the prompt, someone manually reads all 25 outputs and compares them to the expected categories by eye. This takes about 40 minutes and happens less and less often as deadlines get tighter.
contentSections.question: What's the actual failure mode here, beyond just being slow?

options.label: The eval set itself is too large and should be trimmed
Manual scoring's cost means the eval gets skipped exactly when time pressure is highest — which is also when a rushed change is most likely to introduce a regression
Categorization tasks can't be automatically scored at all

feedback.toolarge: 25 cases is a reasonable size per the previous lesson — the problem isn't the set's size, it's that checking it costs 40 minutes of manual comparison every single time, which is a scoring-method problem, not a set-size problem.
feedback.skipped_under_pressure: Right. This is the actual danger: an eval that takes real manual effort every run gets skipped precisely under the conditions — deadline pressure, a change that needs to ship fast — where a regression is most likely to slip through unnoticed, which is exactly backwards from when the safety net is needed most.
feedback.cant_score: Categorization is actually one of the easiest task types to score automatically — the model's output category can be directly, mechanically compared against the known-correct category string, no human judgment required at all.

contentSections.mechanism: **The right question for any eval case isn't "can a human check this" — it's "can a computer check this without a human, and if so, why isn't it doing that already."** For a category, a yes/no field, an extracted number, or any output where the known-correct answer is a specific, comparable value, automated scoring is exactly the kind of exact-match comparison the first module of this phase established works fine on constrained, non-free-text output. Building that comparison once, as code, is what makes an eval cheap enough to run on every change instead of skipped when time is tight.

contentSections.body: This is where the eval harness stops being a manual process and becomes an actual harness: a script that runs each case's input through the current version of the tool, compares the output to the known-correct answer using an appropriate check (exact match for a category or extracted value, a numeric tolerance for a computed number, a substring or structural check for a constrained format), and reports a pass/fail or a score per case plus an aggregate. Once that exists, running the full eval set costs seconds of compute time and zero minutes of anyone's attention — which is the only way it survives contact with a real deadline.

An eval that requires manual comparison every run gets skipped exactly when a deadline makes it most needed — automating the comparison for anything with a checkable, specific expected value is what makes an eval survive contact with real time pressure.

contentSections.title: Where automated scoring runs out

contentSections.body: Not every output has a single checkable expected value. A summary, an explanation, a piece of generated code with more than one valid implementation — these don't reduce to a clean exact-match comparison, and pretending they do produces a scorer that's either too strict or too loose to mean anything.

contentSections.question: What's wrong with this scoring function for a free-text summary task?

options.label: It requires the summary to match a reference string exactly, which fails the same way exact-match assertions failed on generative output in the first module of this phase
It should trim more aggressively
Summaries can't be scored by any automated method, ever

feedback.trim: Whitespace handling isn't the issue here — even a perfectly-trimmed, semantically correct summary that's phrased even slightly differently from the reference string will score 0.
feedback.exactmatch: Right. This is the exact same mistake the phase opened with, now showing up inside a scoring function instead of a test assertion: a correct summary phrased differently from the one reference answer gets scored as completely wrong, which will produce misleading, noisy comparisons between versions that are actually both fine.
feedback.never: Free text isn't unscorable — it needs a different kind of check than exact match, which is exactly what the second half of this lesson is about, not an admission that nothing automated can help here at all.

contentSections.flawExplanation: Applying exact-match scoring to free text repeats the phase's opening mistake at the scoring-function level. What actually works for free text, in order of effort and reliability: **property checks that are themselves automatable** (does the summary mention every action item name that appears in the source, checked as a substring or keyword match — genuinely checkable by code, without needing exact wording); and where that's not enough, **model-graded scoring** — using a separate model call to judge the output against a rubric, which is faster than a human but needs its own validation, since it inherits its own judgment reliability questions. Free text that resists both of these genuinely needs the sampled human review the next lesson covers — which is the honest admission that not everything should be forced into an automated score just because automation is convenient.

contentSections.body: A workable rule of thumb: score automatically wherever the correct answer reduces to a specific, comparable value or a checkable property (categories, extracted fields, presence of required content) — this covers more of a typical tool's eval set than it first appears, since even summarization tasks usually have *some* checkable properties (are the real action items present, is there no invented commitment) even though the exact wording isn't checkable. Reserve human or model-graded review for the genuinely subjective remainder — tone, phrasing quality, overall usefulness — rather than defaulting to it for everything free-text just because it's less work to set up an automated property check.

Exact-match scoring on free text repeats this phase's opening mistake at the scoring-function level — score automatically what reduces to a checkable property, and reserve human or model-graded review for the genuinely subjective remainder.

title: Sampling for human review where you can't
description: Why forcing a genuinely subjective quality into an automated proxy metric measures close to nothing real, and how to build a representative, rubric-based sampled review process instead.

learningObjectives.text: Recognize when a quality dimension resists automated scoring and needs human judgment instead
Design a representative, rubric-based sampled review process with a real cadence

contentSections.title: The remainder that can't be automated away

contentSections.body: After building automated scoring for everything that reduces to a checkable property, a real remainder is usually still left — whether a summary's tone is appropriate, whether a generated explanation is actually clear to a non-expert, whether a response would land well with a specific customer. None of that reduces to a property check, and pretending it does just moves the exact-match mistake one level up.

contentSections.scenario: A team trying to fully automate their marketing-copy eval writes a property check: "does the output contain at least one of these approved power words (amazing, revolutionary, game-changing)." They score every generated headline against this checklist and treat a high score as evidence of good copy.
contentSections.question: What's wrong with this approach?

options.label: It reduces genuine quality — persuasiveness, brand fit, whether it's actually good writing — to a keyword checklist that a headline can pass while being bad, or fail while being excellent
The specific power words chosen are the wrong ones
Nothing — a checklist score is just as valid as any other measurement

feedback.wordchoice: Swapping in different power words doesn't fix the underlying problem — any fixed keyword list has the same failure mode: a genuinely great headline that happens not to use any of them scores zero, and a genuinely bad, cliché-stuffed headline that hits three of them scores high.
feedback.reduces: Right. This is what happens when a team tries to force something genuinely subjective into an automated property check because automation is more convenient than admitting a human judgment is needed. The checklist measures keyword presence, which correlates only loosely, if at all, with actual quality — and optimizing toward the checklist can make the copy worse in exactly the way it makes the metric look better.
feedback.valid: A measurement that doesn't actually track the thing you care about isn't just a weaker measurement — it's actively misleading, because it looks like data while measuring something close to unrelated to real quality.

contentSections.concept: **The honest response to a genuinely subjective quality is sampling for human review, not inventing a proxy metric that's easier to compute.** This is the direct sibling of the earlier module's lesson on matching testing effort to what a component actually needs — forcing automation onto something that needs judgment produces a number that looks rigorous and measures close to nothing real, which is worse than admitting the limit and building a real (if smaller-scale) human review process instead.

contentSections.body: Sampled human review doesn't mean reading every output by hand forever — it means applying the same discipline the earlier module used for real API calls in CI: a small, deliberate, representative sample, reviewed against an explicit rubric (not a vague "does this feel good"), on a regular but bounded cadence. For the marketing-copy example, that might mean pulling 10 generated headlines after each significant prompt change, having a human rate each against 3-4 specific rubric criteria (clarity, brand voice match, absence of overused clichés, would-a-real-customer-click), and tracking that rating over time — smaller in scope than reviewing everything, but honest about what it's actually measuring.

A proxy metric invented to avoid admitting something needs human judgment measures close to nothing real — sampling a small, representative set for human review against an explicit rubric is the honest alternative.

contentSections.title: Making the sample actually representative

contentSections.body: A sampled review is only as good as what gets sampled — and the easy failure mode is reviewing whatever's convenient (the most recent outputs, or the ones someone happened to notice) rather than a set that actually represents the tool's real range.

contentSections.intro: You're designing the sampled human-review process for the marketing-copy tool's subjective quality dimensions.

fields.prompt: How should the sample of headlines to review be chosen?
options: A mix: some drawn from the fixed eval set for consistency across time, plus some randomly sampled from recent real usage to catch what the fixed set doesn't cover
Whatever the reviewer happens to remember seeing that looked interesting
Only the headlines that got the most clicks, since those are the successes worth understanding
fields.correctValue: A mix: some drawn from the fixed eval set for consistency across time, plus some randomly sampled from recent real usage to catch what the fixed set doesn't cover

feedback.A mix: some drawn from the fixed eval se: Right — the fixed-set portion lets you compare the same cases over time the way lesson one's fixed eval set does, while the random-recent portion catches real usage patterns and edge cases the fixed set doesn't anticipate.
feedback.Whatever the reviewer happens to remembe: This is memory-driven selection bias — 'looked interesting' skews toward whatever was notable for good or bad reasons, not toward what's actually representative of typical output.
feedback.Only the headlines that got the most cli: This only samples successes, telling you nothing about the failures or mediocre cases that a real quality process needs to catch — a representative sample has to include the full range, not just the winners.

fields.prompt: What should the reviewer be given to work from?
options: An explicit rubric with 3-5 specific, named criteria, each with a clear description of what a good score looks like
A blank space to write general impressions
A single overall 1-10 quality score with no further guidance
fields.correctValue: An explicit rubric with 3-5 specific, named criteria, each with a clear description of what a good score looks like

feedback.An explicit rubric with 3-5 specific, na: Right — an explicit rubric is what turns 'human review' from a vague vibe-check into something consistent enough to compare across reviewers and across time, the same discipline the earlier phase modules applied to labs and self-checks.
feedback.A blank space to write general impressio: Unstructured impressions are hard to compare across different reviewers or across time — two reviewers might weight completely different things without a shared rubric to anchor them.
feedback.A single overall 1-10 quality score with: A single undefined number hides what's actually being measured and makes it impossible to tell whether a score changed because of tone, clarity, brand fit, or something else entirely — specific criteria are what make the score actionable.

fields.prompt: How often should this sampled review actually happen?
options: After every significant prompt or model change, plus a smaller regular check even when nothing's changed, to catch drift
Only once, when the tool first launches
Continuously, on every single output, by a rotating team member
fields.correctValue: After every significant prompt or model change, plus a smaller regular check even when nothing's changed, to catch drift

feedback.After every significant prompt or model: Right — this mirrors the earlier module's scheduled drift-check reasoning: review specifically at the moments most likely to introduce a change, plus a smaller ongoing check for the kind of silent drift (a model update behind an unchanged version string) that doesn't correspond to any deliberate change on the team's part.
feedback.Only once, when the tool first launches: This misses every regression introduced after launch — exactly the gap a one-time email or one-time training session left in the earlier module's edge-case checklist lesson.
feedback.Continuously, on every single output, by: This reintroduces the full manual-review cost problem from the start of this lesson — full coverage by continuous human review doesn't scale and will get skipped under pressure exactly like the earlier manual-scoring example.

contentSections.synthesis: A sampled review process that actually works combines representative selection (not just convenient or successful examples), an explicit shared rubric (not a vague impression), and a deliberate cadence tied to both real changes and ongoing drift — the same three disciplines (representativeness, explicitness, and scheduled checking) that have shown up throughout this module and the one before it, now applied specifically to the quality dimension that can't be automated away.

contentSections.body: A sampled human review needs representative selection (not just convenient examples), an explicit rubric (not a vague impression), and a deliberate cadence tied to real changes plus ongoing drift-checking.

title: Running the harness before every real change
description: Why an eval harness run only occasionally can't localize a regression to a specific cause, and how to trigger it on exactly the changes that could plausibly affect real output behavior.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why infrequent eval runs make regressions hard to attribute to a specific change
Identify which categories of change should trigger an eval harness run

contentSections.title: The harness that only runs when someone remembers

contentSections.body: A team builds a genuinely good eval harness — a fixed, representative case set, automated scoring where it fits, a sampled review process for the rest — and then runs it roughly whenever someone thinks of it. Three prompt changes ship between eval runs. When a regression finally gets caught, nobody can tell which of the three changes caused it.

contentSections.scenario: The eval harness exists, works correctly, and takes under two minutes to run. It caught two real regressions in its first month. Since then, it's been run four times in three months, not tied to any specific event, while dozens of prompt and code changes shipped in the same period.
contentSections.question: What's the actual problem, given the harness itself works fine?

options.label: The harness isn't run close enough to each individual change to attribute a regression to a specific cause
The harness needs to be rebuilt from scratch
Four times in three months is actually a reasonable cadence

feedback.rebuild: Nothing about the harness's actual function is broken — it caught two real regressions when it was run. The problem is entirely about when and how often it gets run, not about its design.
feedback.not_per_change: Right. With dozens of changes shipping between four eval runs, a regression found on the fourth run could have been introduced by any of dozens of intervening changes — which is exactly the localization problem the earlier module's whole bug-diagnosis process depends on avoiding. Running the harness right before or after each specific change is what makes a regression attributable to one cause instead of a pile of suspects.
feedback.reasonable: Four times in three months against dozens of shipped changes means most changes never got checked at all before or immediately after shipping — that's not a reasonable safety margin, it's closer to spot-checking after the fact.

contentSections.mechanism: **An eval harness that isn't run close to every real change provides much less protection than its existence suggests, and makes any regression it does catch much harder to localize.** This directly extends the previous module's reproduce-before-you-fix discipline: a regression found four eval-runs-worth of changes after it was introduced is in exactly the position the phase's third module opened with — a bug that's hard to reproduce and even harder to isolate, except this time it was avoidable, because the harness that would have caught it immediately already existed and just wasn't run.

contentSections.body: The fix is making the harness part of the actual shipping process, not an optional extra step someone has to remember. For most teams that means: run it automatically before merging any change that touches the prompt, the model configuration, or logic that affects the eval-covered feature — as a required CI step, the same way the mocked test suite from the earlier module runs on every push. Fast, automated scoring is what makes this affordable; a harness that takes 40 minutes of manual comparison per run, per the earlier lesson, could never survive being run on every single change, which is exactly why building the automated scoring first is a prerequisite for this lesson's advice actually working.

A harness run occasionally, disconnected from individual changes, can't localize a regression to a specific cause — running it automatically before every real change is what makes both prevention and diagnosis actually work.

contentSections.title: What "before every real change" actually means

contentSections.body: "Before every real change" doesn't mean every single commit, including a typo fix in a comment — that would reintroduce the exact friction and skipped-under-pressure problem lesson two already diagnosed for manual scoring. It means every change that could plausibly affect the model's behavior.

contentSections.scenario: A team is deciding which of these changes should trigger the eval harness automatically before merge.
contentSections.question: Select every change below that should trigger the eval harness, because it could plausibly affect the tool's actual output behavior.

items.label: Any edit to the prompt template
Bumping the configured model version
Fixing a typo in a code comment unrelated to any prompt or logic
Changing the logic that assembles context (retrieval, data lookups) for the request
Updating the README's installation instructions
Changing how the model's response gets parsed and validated

explanation.prompt: A direct edit to what's sent to the model is exactly the kind of change most likely to shift behavior — this is the clearest possible trigger.
explanation.model: A different model version can behave meaningfully differently even against an unchanged prompt, and per the earlier module, even an unannounced provider-side update behind a stable version string is a real risk worth an eval run to catch.
explanation.comment: A comment change has zero effect on runtime behavior — triggering a full eval run for this would be exactly the kind of friction that eventually gets the check disabled or ignored out of frustration.
explanation.contextlogic: This is the previous module's 'context' suspect directly — a change to what data gets assembled into the request can shift output just as much as a prompt edit, and deserves the same trigger.
explanation.readme: Documentation changes don't touch runtime behavior at all — no reason to run an eval that measures actual tool output.
explanation.parsing: A parsing or validation change sits downstream of the model call, but a bug introduced there can still change what the tool ultimately does with a correct model response — worth triggering the harness to catch that class of regression too.

contentSections.synthesis: The dividing line is whether a change could plausibly affect what the tool actually does when it runs — prompt, model version, context-assembly logic, and response-handling logic all qualify; comments and documentation don't. This is the same proportionality this whole phase has argued for repeatedly: match the check to what's actually at risk, not to every possible change regardless of relevance.

contentSections.body: This closes the loop the whole phase has been building toward. A fast, automated, representative eval harness — the product of this module's first three lessons — is only as valuable as the discipline of actually running it at the moments that matter, which is this lesson's contribution, and the final lesson closes with what happens when it catches something real.

Trigger the eval harness on anything that could plausibly affect actual output behavior — prompt, model version, context logic, response parsing — not on every commit regardless of relevance, or the check becomes friction people route around.

title: Catching a regression before a user does
description: What actually happens when a well-built eval harness catches a real regression before shipping, and why the harness itself needs the same ongoing maintenance this phase has argued for throughout.

learningObjectives.text: Apply the eval harness's finding to diagnose and confirm a fix for a caught regression
Explain why a fixed eval set needs periodic updates as a tool's real functionality grows

contentSections.title: What the harness actually earns you

contentSections.body: Everything in this module has been building toward one moment: a change ships, the harness catches a real drop in quality before any user ever sees it, and the team finds out from a dashboard instead of from a support queue. This is the payoff the whole phase — testing, mocking, debugging, edge cases, evaluation — has been assembling.

contentSections.title: The regression the harness catches
contentSections.opening: A prompt change ships to the ticket-summarizer, intended to make summaries more concise. The eval harness runs automatically as part of the merge process. The automated scoring shows action-item completeness dropped from 96% to 71% on the fixed eval set — a real, specific, quantified drop, not a vague impression.

found.situation: The number is right there: 96% to 71%. The PR is still open, unmerged. Nobody outside the team has seen either version yet.
found.question: What's the right next step?

choices.label: Merge anyway — the summaries do look more concise, and 71% is probably still fine
choices.consequence: The regression ships. Within days, support tickets about missed action items start climbing — the exact failure mode the harness was built to catch, now happening in production instead of in a PR.

choices.label: Pull the specific cases that dropped from pass to fail, and diagnose why, using the previous module's prompt/context/model isolation process
choices.consequence: You find the new prompt's push toward conciseness is causing the model to drop action items that aren't in the first two sentences of a ticket — a specific, fixable cause, isolated before anything ships.

choices.label: Revert the change entirely and abandon the conciseness goal
choices.consequence: The regression is avoided, but so is the original, reasonable goal of more concise summaries — the team never learns what specifically went wrong or whether a narrower version of the change could have worked.

shipped_anyway.summary: The harness caught the regression and it shipped anyway — the measurement existed, and the discipline to act on it didn't.
shipped_anyway.lesson: A number that gets overridden by a vibe ("the summaries look more concise") is exactly the failure this whole module was built to prevent, now happening one step later than usual — not from lacking a measurement, but from not trusting the measurement over an impression, which is the very first lesson of this module, restated at the moment it mattered most.

diagnosed.summary: The specific failing cases get isolated, the actual cause identified, and a narrower fix that keeps most of the conciseness gain without the action-item drop gets written and re-checked against the same eval set.
diagnosed.lesson: This is the whole phase working together: the harness caught the regression with a real number, the previous module's isolation process found the actual cause, and the fix gets confirmed against the same fixed eval set before shipping — closing the loop from 'a vague sense it's fine' all the way to a specific, measured, fixed problem.

reverted.summary: The regression is avoided, at the cost of the entire improvement and any understanding of what specifically went wrong.
reverted.lesson: Reverting protects against the immediate harm but wastes the diagnostic value the eval harness was built to provide — it caught something specific and fixable, and abandoning the whole change instead of isolating the actual cause throws that specificity away.

contentSections.body: The "diagnosed" path is the one this whole phase has been building toward — not a single technique but a compounding one. The eval harness (this module) catches a real, quantified problem before shipping. The prompt/context/model isolation process (the earlier module) finds the actual cause instead of guessing. The near-neighbor regression discipline (also from that module) confirms the fix didn't just move the problem. And the fixed eval set itself, run again after the fix, is the final confirmation — the same tool that caught the regression is what proves it's actually resolved.

An eval harness earns its cost at exactly the moment a real regression shows up as a number before a user ever sees it — and what happens next depends on trusting that number over an impression, and using it to diagnose rather than just react.

contentSections.title: Keeping the harness itself honest

contentSections.body: The harness that catches today's regression can itself go stale in exactly the ways this whole phase has warned about — a fixture that no longer matches reality, a checklist nobody consults, a fixed eval set that stops representing what the tool actually needs to handle as the tool and its real usage evolve.

contentSections.scenario: A team's eval set was built 18 months ago, when the tool handled three ticket categories. The tool now handles nine categories, added gradually over that time, with no corresponding updates to the eval set.
contentSections.question: Roughly what share of the tool's current real functionality does that 18-month-old eval set still actually cover?
contentSections.actualValue: unpredictable, and often much less than assumed — potentially as low as a third
contentSections.explanation: There's no fixed number worth memorizing here — the point is that a fixed eval set is fixed in exactly the way that made it valuable (stable, comparable across time), and that same fixedness means it doesn't automatically grow to cover new functionality on its own. A set built for three categories, unchanged while six more got added, is now silently blind to two-thirds of what the tool does — the same staleness risk the earlier module's fixture-drift lesson described, now at the level of the eval set itself rather than a single mocked response.

contentSections.body: The fix is the same shape as the earlier module's scheduled drift-check, applied to the eval set instead of a fixture library: periodically — whenever a genuinely new capability ships, or on a standing quarterly review if nothing else prompts it — add representative cases for whatever's new, and prune or update cases that no longer reflect how the tool is actually used. This isn't a one-time build followed by permanent maintenance-free operation; it's a living asset that needs the same kind of ongoing attention the phase has argued for throughout, applied one level up, to the measurement tool itself rather than to the tool it measures.

A fixed eval set is fixed in the sense of stable-for-comparison, not in the sense of permanently complete — it needs periodic updates as the tool's real functionality grows, or it silently stops covering what the tool actually does.

title: Lab — Build and run an eval harness on your tool
description: Build a minimal but real eval harness — a fixed case set, automated scoring, and a before/after comparison — for one real AI-powered feature.

learningObjectives.text: Construct a fixed, representative eval case set with verified expected outcomes
Compare two versions of a feature using automated scoring and interpret the results

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: This is the phase's capstone lab: build a real eval harness for a real AI-powered feature, run it against two versions, and see what it actually tells you — which is the point of everything this whole phase has built toward.

contentSections.title: Build and run an eval harness on your tool
contentSections.brief: Take one real AI-powered feature — ideally one you've already worked with in this phase's earlier labs. Build a minimal but real eval harness for it: a fixed case set, automated scoring where possible, and a run against two versions of the feature (before and after some real or deliberately-introduced change) to see what the harness actually reveals.
contentSections.deliverable: A harness with a real test set, run against two versions, results compared.

stages.title: Build the fixed case set
stages.instructions: Build 8-15 representative cases spanning your feature's real difficulty range, each with a hand-verified known-correct or known-acceptable outcome. Include at least 2 edge cases from the earlier module's categories.
stages.checkpoint: Every case has a specific, verified expected outcome, and the set includes at least one easy, one hard, and one edge case.

stages.title: Build automated scoring for what's checkable
stages.instructions: For every case whose expected outcome reduces to a specific value or checkable property, write a script that runs the case through your tool and automatically scores it. Note explicitly which cases, if any, resist automated scoring and would need human review instead.
stages.checkpoint: The script runs and produces a pass/fail or score for every automatable case, with zero manual comparison required.

stages.title: Make a real or deliberate change, and run both versions
stages.instructions: Either use a real recent change to the feature, or deliberately introduce one (a prompt tweak, a different instruction). Run your eval harness against both the before and after versions on the exact same case set.
stages.checkpoint: You have two sets of results — before and after — on the identical case set, not two different samples.

stages.title: Compare and write up what the harness found
stages.instructions: Compare the before/after results. Did anything get better, worse, or stay the same? If something regressed, name which specific cases and, if you can, why (using the previous module's prompt/context/model isolation). Write this up as a short report.
stages.checkpoint: The write-up states a specific before/after comparison with real numbers, not a general impression of which version seemed better.

rubric.criterion: The case set is fixed, representative, and has verified expected outcomes
rubric.meets: 8-15 cases spanning easy/hard/edge difficulty, each with a specific, hand-verified expected answer.

rubric.criterion: Automated scoring exists and requires no manual comparison
rubric.meets: A script runs every automatable case and produces a score without a human reading each output.

rubric.criterion: The comparison uses the identical case set for both versions
rubric.meets: Before and after results come from running the same fixed cases, not two different samples.

rubric.criterion: The report states specific numbers, not general impressions
rubric.meets: The write-up cites actual pass/fail counts or scores, not 'it seemed better/worse.'

rubric.criterion: Any regression found is named specifically
rubric.meets: If something got worse, the specific failing case and a hypothesis for why are stated, not just 'some things regressed.'

rubric.criterion: The remainder that resists automated scoring is acknowledged honestly
rubric.meets: Cases that would need human review are explicitly named as such, not silently force-fit into an automated check.

contentSections.body: A real eval harness, even a small one, turns 'I think this is better' into a number you can defend — which is the whole phase's argument, made concrete on one real tool.

description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from Handling Edge Cases, two from further back. Ungraded, untimed.

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck

questions.from: This module — Building an Eval Harness
questions.prompt: Why doesn't a handful of examples that 'look better' to a few reviewers count as a real evaluation?

options.label: Because it's a judgment about style and impression, not a checkable measurement of whether the output is actually correct
Because reviewers are never qualified to judge AI output
Because it takes too long to gather examples

questions.explanation: An impression of a few examples measures how they read, not whether they're actually correct on a representative, checkable set — exactly the gap that let a real regression through in the module's opening scenario.

questions.from: This module — Building an Eval Harness
questions.prompt: Why does forcing exact-match scoring onto free-text output repeat an earlier mistake?

options.label: Because a correct answer phrased differently gets scored as wrong, the same failure exact-match assertions had on generative output in the phase's first module
Because free text can never be automatically scored at all
Because exact-match scoring is always faster to compute

questions.explanation: This repeats the phase's opening lesson at the scoring-function level — the fix is automated property checks or sampled review, not exact-match on free text.

questions.from: This module — Building an Eval Harness
questions.prompt: What's the honest response to a quality dimension that resists automated scoring?

options.label: A representative, rubric-based sampled human review, not an invented proxy metric or skipping it entirely
Force it into a keyword-checklist metric, since some measurement is better than none
Skip evaluating that dimension entirely

questions.explanation: A proxy metric that doesn't track real quality is actively misleading, and skipping evaluation entirely leaves that dimension free to degrade unnoticed — sampled review is the genuine middle path.

questions.from: This module — Building an Eval Harness
questions.prompt: Why should an eval harness run automatically before every behavior-relevant change rather than occasionally?

options.label: Because infrequent runs make a regression hard to attribute to a specific cause among many intervening changes
Because it needs to run constantly regardless of what changed
Because occasional runs are actually sufficient as long as they happen weekly

questions.explanation: A regression found after many intervening changes can't be cleanly localized to one cause — running the harness close to each relevant change is what preserves that attribution.

questions.from: Previous module — Handling Edge Cases
questions.prompt: Why is silent degradation more dangerous than a visible error?

options.label: Because the user has no way to know the result is incomplete and will likely trust it as complete
Because errors are always logged automatically
It isn't — silent degradation is always the safest default

questions.explanation: A silent partial result looks like a complete, trustworthy one, which is what makes it more dangerous than an honest, visible failure.

questions.from: Previous module — Handling Edge Cases
questions.prompt: What's the difference between output validity and output correctness?

options.label: Validity checks whether output is well-formed; correctness checks whether it's actually right — schema checks can only verify the first
They're the same thing
Correctness is a subset of validity

questions.explanation: An off-by-one error or a wrong-but-allowed category can be perfectly valid while still being substantively wrong.

questions.from: Previous module — Handling Edge Cases
questions.prompt: Why is structural system/user channel separation a more durable defense than blocking specific adversarial phrases?

options.label: Because phrase-blocking is a losing game against endless rephrasing, while channel separation removes the mechanism regardless of wording
Because phrase-blocking is technically impossible
Because channel separation blocks all adversarial content everywhere

questions.explanation: Channel separation doesn't depend on recognizing specific wording, making it durable against rephrasing — though content smuggled inside documents needs its own defense.

questions.from: Previous module — Handling Edge Cases
questions.prompt: Why does a large but format-narrow test set still miss real bugs?

options.label: Because sample-size variety and format/convention variety are different axes
Because large test sets are always slower to run
Because format diversity doesn't affect model behavior

questions.explanation: More examples of one format convention don't add coverage of a different one — format diversity has to be deliberately included.

questions.from: Module two — Mocking Claude in Tests
questions.prompt: What question can a real API call in CI answer that a mock structurally cannot?

options.label: Whether the live model's current judgment is still good on real inputs
Whether the request-building code is correct
Whether the database write succeeds

questions.explanation: Everything else is plumbing a fixture answers just as well — only current live judgment quality needs an actual real call.

questions.from: Module three — Debugging Bad Output
questions.prompt: What are the three suspects for isolating a bad-output regression?

options.label: The prompt, the context, and the model
The frontend, the backend, and the database
The user, the developer, and the provider

questions.explanation: These three categories are what a regression should be isolated to before attempting a fix.
